planned.name: Microsoft Cloud and AI Security Engineer Associate

cards.front: What is cloud computing?
cards.back: Computing services (servers, storage, databases, networking, software) delivered over the internet, on demand, billed for what you use.

cards.front: Public cloud: who owns the hardware, and what do you pay?
cards.back: The provider owns and runs it; hardware is shared. No upfront hardware cost, pay as you go, easy to scale. You get less control.

cards.front: Private cloud: what are its characteristics?
cards.back: Used by one organization. You buy and maintain the hardware (CapEx), and you control the resources and security. Fits strict compliance needs.

cards.front: Hybrid cloud: what is it and when do you use it?
cards.back: Public and private connected, with workloads moving between them. Keep sensitive data on-premises, use the public cloud for extra capacity. Azure Arc manages both sides.

cards.front: “Hardware must be purchased.” Public, private or hybrid?
cards.back: Private. (“Pay only for what you use” and quick provisioning are public cloud traits.)

cards.front: What is serverless?
cards.back: You run code or logic and the provider manages the servers. It scales automatically and bills for execution time. Example: Azure Functions. Servers still exist; you just don't manage them.

cards.front: Name two cloud advantages that come from geo-distribution.
cards.back: Deploy to regional datacenters near users (better performance) and keep running if one region fails.

cards.front: What is the consumption-based model?
cards.back: Pay only for what you use. No upfront cost, and the bill stops when usage stops. It is an OpEx model.

cards.front: CapEx or OpEx: “upfront, one-time spend such as buying hardware”?
cards.back: CapEx (capital expenditure). OpEx is spending as you go, billed by use, with no upfront cost.

cards.front: Why is the cloud often cheaper than an on-premises datacenter?
cards.back: You are billed only for what you use, with no hardware to buy, house, power or maintain.

cards.front: Compare pay-as-you-go and commitment-based pricing.
cards.back: Pay-as-you-go: flexible, no commitment, best for variable or short-term use. Commitment (reservations, savings plans, 1 or 3 years): lower unit price, best for steady, predictable use.

cards.front: What does Azure Hybrid Benefit do?
cards.back: Lets you reuse existing Windows Server and SQL Server licenses (with Software Assurance) in Azure to reduce cost.

cards.front: Shared responsibility: what does Microsoft ALWAYS own?
cards.back: The physical datacenter, physical network and physical hosts.

cards.front: Shared responsibility: what do YOU ALWAYS own?
cards.back: Your information and data, devices, and accounts and identities.

cards.front: Who manages the OS in IaaS, PaaS and SaaS?
cards.back: IaaS: you. PaaS: Microsoft. SaaS: Microsoft.

cards.front: Who manages the application in IaaS, PaaS and SaaS?
cards.back: IaaS: you. PaaS: you. SaaS: Microsoft.

cards.front: What is IaaS and what are its examples and use cases?
cards.back: Rent infrastructure: VMs, storage, virtual networks. You manage the OS, apps and data. Use for lift and shift, test and dev, datacenter extension. Examples: Azure VMs, virtual networks.

cards.front: What is PaaS and what are its examples?
cards.back: Build and run apps without managing servers or the OS. You manage your app and data. Examples: App Service, Azure SQL Database, Cosmos DB, Azure Functions.

cards.front: What is SaaS and how is it usually paid for?
cards.back: Finished software hosted and managed for you, used over the internet, usually licensed by monthly or annual subscription. Example: Microsoft 365.

cards.front: Your developers want to focus on building the app, not managing servers. Which service type?
cards.back: PaaS.

cards.front: Is Azure Cosmos DB IaaS, PaaS or SaaS? And Azure VMs?
cards.back: Cosmos DB: PaaS. Azure VMs: IaaS.

cards.front: What does high availability depend on in the public cloud?
cards.back: The service-level agreement (SLA). Different services and tiers have different SLAs.

cards.front: Scalability vs elasticity?
cards.back: Scalability: you can add or remove resources to handle load. Elasticity: it happens automatically and quickly with demand, in and back out.

cards.front: Scale up or scale out: adding more VMs to handle load?
cards.back: Scale out (horizontal scaling). Scale up (vertical) = a bigger VM with more CPU or RAM.

cards.front: Which benefit comes from spreading resources across multiple Azure regions?
cards.back: High availability (resilience to a regional outage). Scalability is about capacity, not location.

cards.front: Cloud backup, data replication and geo-distribution are features of which plan?
cards.back: A disaster recovery plan.

cards.front: Reliability: what three ideas?
cards.back: Resiliency, redundancy and failover. Predictability covers performance (autoscaling, load balancing, high availability) and cost.

cards.front: How do you calculate a composite SLA?
cards.back: Multiply the SLAs of the services together. It is always lower than the lowest single SLA. Example: 99.9% × 99.95% ≈ 99.85%.

cards.front: Downtime per year at 99%, 99.9% and 99.99%?
Management OF the cloud vs management IN the cloud?
cards.back: Of: autoscaling, deploying from templates, monitoring and alerts. In: using the portal, CLI, PowerShell and APIs to manage your resources.

cards.front: Security and governance in the cloud: who is responsible?
cards.back: Responsibility is shared. The provider supplies security tools and compliance; governance sets your standards and policies.

cards.front: What is an availability zone?
cards.back: A physically separate datacenter (or group of datacenters) inside one Azure region, with independent power, cooling and networking.

cards.front: What is a region pair?
cards.back: Two regions in the same geography, at least 300 miles apart, used for disaster recovery. Microsoft updates paired regions one at a time.

cards.front: A region pair is always within the same what?
cards.back: The same geography (for example US or Europe). Not the same availability zone.

cards.front: Region, availability zone, geography: which contains which?
cards.back: Geography > region > availability zones > datacenters.

cards.front: Zonal, zone-redundant and non-regional services: what are they?
cards.back: Zonal: you pin a resource to one zone. Zone-redundant: replicated across zones automatically. Non-regional: not tied to a region (for example Entra ID).

cards.front: What are sovereign regions?
cards.back: Instances isolated from the main Azure instance for compliance or legal reasons, such as Azure Government (US) and Azure China 21Vianet.

cards.front: Order the Azure hierarchy from top to bottom.
cards.back: Management groups > subscriptions > resource groups > resources.

cards.front: What is a resource? Is a storage account named storage001 a resource or a resource group?
cards.back: A resource is a manageable item such as a VM, storage account, web app, database or VNet. storage001 is a resource.

cards.front: Resource group rules to know.
cards.back: A resource lives in exactly one group. Groups cannot nest. Deleting a group deletes everything in it. Access, policy and locks applied to a group apply to current and future resources.

cards.front: What are the two jobs of a subscription?
cards.back: A billing boundary and an access-control boundary. Subscriptions hold resource groups and resources.

cards.front: What do management groups do, and how do they differ from administrative units?
cards.back: Management groups apply access, policy and compliance across multiple subscriptions. Administrative units delegate admin of Microsoft Entra resources (users, groups), not Azure resources.

cards.front: Management group limits.
cards.back: Up to 6 levels of depth (not counting root or subscription level), 10,000 per directory, and each has one parent.

cards.front: What is Azure Resource Manager (ARM)?
cards.back: The deployment and management service for Azure. Every tool (portal, CLI, PowerShell, APIs) goes through it, so you get consistent results, access control, locks and tags.

cards.front: Virtual machines: service type and your responsibility?
cards.back: IaaS. You patch and update the OS and software inside the VM.

cards.front: VM size letters.
cards.back: B burstable, D general purpose, E memory optimized, F compute optimized, M large memory, L storage optimized, N GPU.

cards.front: Virtual machine scale set: what is it?
cards.back: A group of identical, load-balanced VMs that scale out and in automatically on demand or a schedule.

cards.front: Availability set: what does it protect against?
cards.back: Hardware failure and planned maintenance within a region, using update domains (reboot together) and fault domains (share power and network). No extra cost.

cards.front: What is Azure Virtual Desktop?
cards.back: A cloud-hosted desktop and app virtualization service, accessible from many devices.

cards.front: Containers vs VMs.
cards.back: Containers share the host OS and start fast and light. VMs each carry a full OS. Azure options: Container Instances (simple, fast), Container Apps (serverless containers), AKS (Kubernetes orchestration).

cards.front: What is Azure App Service?
cards.back: A PaaS platform for hosting web apps, APIs and mobile backends without managing servers.

cards.front: What is Azure Functions?
cards.back: Serverless, event-driven code. Runs when triggered (timer, HTTP, queue) and scales automatically.

cards.front: Which resources does a VM need?
cards.back: The VM itself plus a disk, a virtual network and subnet, a network interface, and usually an IP address and network security rules.

cards.front: What is a virtual network (VNet)?
cards.back: Your private network in Azure. Resources inside communicate with each other, the internet and on-premises, and you divide it into subnets.

cards.front: How do you let two virtual networks communicate?
cards.back: VNet peering, over Microsoft's backbone as if they were one network.

cards.front: What is VPN Gateway used for?
cards.back: An encrypted tunnel over the public internet that connects an on-premises datacenter to an Azure VNet (site-to-site), one device to a VNet (point-to-site), or two VNets (VNet-to-VNet).

cards.front: VPN Gateway high availability options.
cards.back: Active/standby (failover in about 90 seconds on unplanned failure), active/active (two tunnels), and zone-redundant gateways.

cards.front: What is ExpressRoute?
cards.back: A private connection to Microsoft through a provider that does not use the public internet. More reliable, faster, lower and steadier latency. DNS queries, certificate revocation checks and CDN requests still use the internet.

cards.front: What is ExpressRoute Global Reach?
cards.back: Connects your own sites to each other through Microsoft's network.

cards.front: VPN Gateway or ExpressRoute: a private line with higher bandwidth and no internet?
cards.back: ExpressRoute.

cards.front: Service endpoint vs private endpoint.
cards.back: Service endpoint: keeps traffic to an Azure service on the Azure backbone, but the service keeps its public address. Private endpoint: gives the service a private IP in your VNet.

cards.front: What connects Azure services such as Azure SQL to a VNet over the backbone?
cards.back: Service endpoints.

cards.front: NSG vs route table (UDR).
cards.back: NSG: allow or deny traffic by source, destination, port and protocol. Route table: overrides Azure's default routing, for example to send traffic through a firewall.

cards.front: What are Azure Firewall, NVA and Bastion?
cards.back: Azure Firewall: managed stateful firewall. NVA: a VM acting as a firewall or router. Bastion: browser-based RDP/SSH to VMs without public IPs.

cards.front: What does Azure DNS offer?
cards.back: Hosts DNS domains on Azure with the same tools, credentials and billing. Anycast routing (nearest server answers), alias records (follow a resource's IP changes), private DNS zones for names inside VNets.

cards.front: Name the five core Azure Storage services.
cards.back: Blobs, Files, Queues, Disks, Tables (BFQDT).

cards.front: What is Blob storage used for?
cards.back: Massive amounts of unstructured data: serving images or documents to a browser, backup and restore, archives, streaming.

cards.front: What is Azure Files and which protocols does it use?
cards.back: Managed cloud file shares that can be mounted as a drive by multiple machines, over SMB and NFS (not FTP).

cards.front: Blob access tiers: which is which?
cards.back: Hot: frequent access, highest storage cost, fastest access. Cool: 30-day minimum. Cold: 90-day minimum. Archive: 180-day minimum, offline, lowest storage cost, highest access cost, must be rehydrated.

cards.front: Which tier cannot be set at the storage account level?
cards.back: Archive (it is set on individual blobs).

cards.front: Storage account name rules.
cards.back: 3 to 24 characters, lowercase letters and numbers only, globally unique.

cards.front: Redundancy options and durability.
cards.back: LRS: one datacenter, 11 nines. ZRS: across zones, 12 nines. GRS and GZRS: another region too, 16 nines. RA-GRS/RA-GZRS add read access to the secondary.

cards.front: Which redundancy survives the loss of an entire region?
cards.back: GRS or GZRS (and their read-access versions).

cards.front: How does geo-redundant replication to the secondary region work?
cards.back: Asynchronously, typically with a recovery point objective under 15 minutes.

cards.front: Tool picker: AzCopy, Storage Explorer, File Sync, Azure Migrate, Data Box.
cards.back: AzCopy: command-line copy (one-way). Storage Explorer: GUI. File Sync: two-way sync of on-premises file servers with Azure Files. Azure Migrate: assess and move servers. Data Box: physical device for large offline transfers (up to 80 TB).

cards.front: What is Microsoft Entra ID?
cards.back: Cloud identity and access management: authentication, SSO, MFA, app and device management. It does not provide traditional AD DS.

cards.front: Microsoft Entra Domain Services vs Entra Connect vs managed identities.
cards.back: Domain Services: managed AD DS (domain join, group policy, LDAP, Kerberos) without domain controllers. Entra Connect: syncs on-premises Active Directory to Entra ID. Managed identities: let Azure apps and resources authenticate to other Azure services without stored credentials.

cards.front: Authentication vs authorization.
cards.back: Authentication proves who you are. Authorization decides what you can do.

cards.front: What is SSO and what is its weakness?
cards.back: Sign in once to reach many apps. It is only as secure as the first sign-in, so pair it with MFA.

cards.front: MFA factors and passwordless options.
cards.back: Something you know, have, or are. Passwordless: Windows Hello for Business, Microsoft Authenticator, FIDO2 security keys.

cards.front: External identities: B2B vs External ID for customers.
cards.back: B2B: partners and guests sign in with their own credentials; you control access. External ID for customers: sign-up and sign-in for your customers' apps (formerly Azure AD B2C).

cards.front: What is Conditional Access?
cards.back: If-then access policies. Signals (user, location, device, risk) lead to a decision (allow, block, require MFA) that is then enforced.

cards.front: What is Azure RBAC?
cards.back: Access control by role at a scope (management group, subscription, resource group, resource). It is an allow model enforced through ARM. Roles: Owner, Contributor, Reader.

cards.front: Zero Trust principles.
cards.back: Verify explicitly, use least privilege access, assume breach.

cards.front: Defense in depth layers.
cards.back: Physical, identity and access, perimeter, network, compute, application, data.

cards.front: Encryption at rest vs in transit; what is Key Vault?
cards.back: At rest: data stored on disk. In transit: data moving over a network. Key Vault: central secure store for secrets, keys and certificates.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud?
cards.back: Monitors security posture across Azure, hybrid and multicloud: assess (secure score and recommendations), secure, defend (threat protection).

cards.front: What can Cost Management + Billing do?
cards.back: Create and manage budgets and alerts, analyze costs, generate reports from historical data and forecast future spend.

cards.front: Which tool estimates what Azure services will cost BEFORE you deploy?
cards.back: The Azure pricing calculator.

cards.front: Which option lowers the cost of VMs with steady usage all year?
cards.back: Azure Reservations (commit for 1 or 3 years; saves up to about 72% versus pay-as-you-go). Savings plans are a flexible commitment alternative.

cards.front: What does a spending limit do?
cards.back: Suspends the subscription when the limit is reached. It does not reduce prices.

cards.front: What are tags?
cards.back: Name-value pairs applied to resources to organize them and track cost by department, project or environment. They are not inherited automatically.

cards.front: What affects Azure costs?
cards.back: Resource type, region, size and usage time, bandwidth (data leaving Azure is charged; data coming in is free), and subscription type.

cards.front: What does Azure Policy do?
cards.back: Creates, assigns and manages rules that audit or enforce resource configuration, such as allowed regions or allowed VM sizes, for new and existing resources. Groups of policies are initiatives.

cards.front: Policy vs RBAC vs locks.
cards.back: RBAC: what users can do. Policy: what resources are allowed to be. Locks (CanNotDelete, ReadOnly): stop accidental deletion or changes, even for owners.

cards.front: What is a resource lock?
cards.back: A protection on a subscription, resource group or resource. Delete (CanNotDelete in the API) lets you read and modify but not delete; ReadOnly allows only reading. Locks inherit down and apply even to Owners, so remove the lock first to make a change.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Purview?
cards.back: Data governance, risk and compliance: discover, classify and protect data across your estate.

cards.front: What can you do in the Azure portal?
cards.back: Browser GUI to create, configure and view resources and reports (and create Entra users). It works from any device with a browser.

cards.front: What is Azure Cloud Shell?
cards.back: A browser-accessible shell with Bash and PowerShell for managing Azure, with no local install.

cards.front: Azure CLI vs PowerShell.
cards.back: Both are command-line ways to manage Azure and script it. CLI uses az commands; PowerShell uses Az cmdlets. Both go through ARM.

cards.front: What is Azure Arc?
cards.back: Extends Azure management, governance and security to servers and resources outside Azure, on-premises or in other clouds, without migrating them.

cards.front: What is infrastructure as code (IaC) and what are ARM templates?
cards.back: IaC: define infrastructure in files so deployments are repeatable and consistent. ARM templates are declarative JSON that describe resources to deploy; Bicep is a simpler language that compiles to them.

cards.front: Azure Advisor: what does it do?
cards.back: Evaluates your Azure resources and recommends improvements for reliability, security, performance, operational excellence and cost.

cards.front: Azure Service Health: what does it do?
cards.back: Notifies you of Azure service problems that affect you, such as a regional outage, and of planned maintenance.

cards.front: Azure Monitor: what does it do?
cards.back: Collects, analyzes and acts on metrics and logs. Builds alerts (for example CPU over 80% for 5 minutes) and can trigger autoscale.

cards.front: Log Analytics and Application Insights?
cards.back: Log Analytics: query and analyze log data. Application Insights: monitors the performance and usage of applications.

cards.front: Advisor, Service Health or Monitor? “Tell me about an Azure outage in my region.”
cards.back: Service Health.

cards.front: Name the six factors that affect Azure costs.
cards.back: Resource type, consumption, maintenance, geography, subscription type, and Azure Marketplace.

cards.front: What are Spot virtual machines?
cards.back: Use unused Azure capacity at a lower price, but Azure can evict them when it needs the capacity back. Best for interruptible, fault-tolerant work such as batch jobs.

cards.front: What is an Azure savings plan for compute?
cards.back: You commit to an hourly spend for 1 or 3 years on eligible compute, and Azure applies the best price. More flexible than reservations because it isn't tied to one VM type.

cards.front: Choose: pay-as-you-go, reservation, savings plan or Spot?
cards.back: Pay-as-you-go: flexible, variable use. Reservation: stable, predictable, specific resources (1 or 3 years). Savings plan: steady spend but flexibility across compute. Spot: interruptible work at the lowest price.

cards.front: Billing zones vs availability zones?
cards.back: A billing zone is a geographic grouping of regions used for data-transfer pricing. It is not an availability zone. Some inbound transfers are free; outbound is priced by zone.

cards.front: What does the pricing calculator do, and what happened to the TCO calculator?
cards.back: The pricing calculator estimates the cost of resources you plan to provision. Nothing is provisioned or charged. The Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculator has been retired.

cards.front: What are the three parts of Cost Management?
cards.back: Cost analysis (view costs by billing cycle, region, resource, subscription, resource group or service), cost alerts, and budgets.

cards.front: Name the three types of cost alerts.
cards.back: Budget alerts (spend reaches a threshold), credit alerts (Azure Prepayment used up, at 90% and 100%), and department spending quota alerts (Enterprise Agreement customers).

cards.front: Can a budget do more than send an alert?
cards.back: Yes. Budgets can trigger automation that suspends or changes resources when a threshold is reached, for example shutting down nonproduction resources.

cards.front: What do tags help with, and how are they managed?
cards.back: Resource management, cost management, operations, security, governance and automation. Managed in the portal, PowerShell, CLI, ARM templates or REST API. Azure Policy can require or reapply tags. Resources do not inherit tags from groups or subscriptions.

cards.front: What does an Azure free account include?
cards.back: Credit to spend in the first 30 days, popular products free for 12 months, and 25+ products that are always free.

cards.front: What are Microsoft Purview's two solution areas?
cards.back: Risk and compliance, and unified data governance. Together they provide automated data discovery, sensitive data classification and end-to-end lineage across on-premises, multicloud and SaaS data.

cards.front: Azure Policy: scope, inheritance and what it evaluates.
cards.back: Set at resource, resource group, subscription or management group level and inherited downward. Evaluates new and existing resources, can block noncompliant ones, and can remediate some (for example adding a missing tag). Resources can be marked as exceptions.

cards.front: What is an Azure Policy initiative?
cards.back: A group of related policy definitions that tracks compliance with a larger goal, for example Enable Monitoring in Azure Security Center (100+ policies).

cards.front: What is the Service Trust Portal?
cards.back: Microsoft's portal for security, privacy and compliance documents and audit reports. You sign in with an Entra work or school account and accept an NDA for some content. My Library saves documents; All Documents lists them.

cards.front: Why can't an Owner change a resource with a ReadOnly lock?
cards.back: Locks apply regardless of RBAC permissions. You must remove the lock first, then perform the action.

cards.front: Azure portal: key facts.
cards.back: A web-based GUI for building, managing and monitoring resources, with custom dashboards and accessibility options. It is resilient, with a presence in every Azure datacenter, and updates without downtime.

cards.front: Azure Cloud Shell: key features.
cards.back: Browser-based shell, no local install, already authenticated with your Azure credentials, and you choose PowerShell or Azure CLI (Bash). Open it from the portal.

cards.front: Azure PowerShell vs Azure CLI?
cards.back: Functionally equivalent. PowerShell runs cmdlets; CLI uses Bash-style commands. Both can be scripted and installed on Windows, Linux and Mac, or used in Cloud Shell. Pick the language you know.

cards.front: What is Copilot in Azure?
cards.back: An AI assistant for administrators that helps explore services, understand options and draft commands or scripts. Validate its recommendations and permissions before applying changes.

cards.front: Which resource types can Azure Arc manage outside Azure?
cards.back: Servers, Kubernetes clusters, Azure data services, SQL Server, and virtual machines (preview). Arc projects them into Azure Resource Manager.

cards.front: Azure Resource Manager: how does a request flow?
cards.back: A request from any tool, API or SDK goes to ARM, which authenticates and authorizes it, then sends it to the Azure service. All tools give consistent results because they share the same API.

cards.front: ARM template benefits.
cards.back: Declarative JSON, repeatable results, orchestration (dependency order and parallel deployment), modularity (nested templates) and extensibility (deployment scripts).

cards.front: What is Bicep?
cards.back: A declarative language for deploying Azure resources through ARM. Simpler and more concise than JSON templates, with idempotent, repeatable deployments and modules.

cards.front: Azure Advisor's five recommendation categories.
cards.back: Reliability, Security, Performance, Operational Excellence and Cost. You can act, postpone or dismiss each one.

cards.front: Service Health: the three views.
cards.back: Azure Status: global health of all services and regions. Service Health: outages, planned maintenance and advisories for the services and regions you use. Resource Health: whether one specific resource (such as a VM) is healthy and whether the problem is Azure's or yours.

cards.front: What are Azure Monitor alerts made of?
cards.back: An alert rule (the condition, metric-based or log-based) and an action group (who is notified and what happens). Action groups are reusable across Monitor, Service Health and Advisor.

cards.front: What is Application Insights?
cards.back: An Azure Monitor feature for the performance and usage of web apps, in Azure, on-premises or another cloud. Tracks requests, response times, failures, dependencies and page views. Add an SDK or enable the agent. Availability tests send synthetic requests.

cards.front: Sustainability in the cloud: what practices does Learn list?
cards.back: Right-size, automate, monitor, keep optimizing. Examples: scale down when demand drops, turn off or deallocate unused resources, pick efficient configurations to avoid overprovisioning, and track usage trends with governance and monitoring. A dev environment that shuts down nights and weekends is the classic example.

cards.front: AI services, Azure Machine Learning or IoT services: how do you choose?
cards.back: Azure AI services: prebuilt AI features (language, speech, vision, documents) through APIs. Azure Machine Learning: build, train and manage your OWN custom models. Azure IoT services: the solution centers on connected devices and telemetry.

cards.front: IoT Hub vs IoT Central vs IoT Edge?
cards.back: IoT Hub: secure two-way communication between cloud services and devices. IoT Central: simplified SaaS IoT platform for solution builders. IoT Edge: runs cloud workloads on devices closer to where the data is generated.

cards.front: What is Azure OpenAI Service, and what is agentic AI at this level?
cards.back: Azure OpenAI Service supports generative AI such as chat and content generation with built-in security and governance. Agentic AI is an application pattern (a model plus instructions, context and tools to finish multistep goals) built from Azure AI services, not a separate compute category.

cards.front: What can Azure App Service host?
cards.back: Web apps, API apps, WebJobs (scheduled or triggered background programs) and mobile app back ends. Windows or Linux, many languages (.NET, Java, PHP, Python, Node.js), automatic scaling, built-in high availability, and continuous deployment from GitHub, Azure DevOps or any Git repo.

cards.front: Hosting spectrum: VMs, containers, App Service?
cards.back: VMs give the most control (and the most to manage). Containers isolate and individually manage parts of the app. App Service gives the least operational effort: you build the app, Azure keeps the environment running.

cards.front: Which Azure services are global, with no region to choose?
cards.back: Microsoft Entra ID, Azure Traffic Manager and Azure DNS. Other services (and some VM sizes and storage types) are only available in certain regions.

cards.front: How many availability zones does a zone-enabled region have?
cards.back: At least three separate zones. Each zone has independent power, cooling and networking, and zones connect over high-speed private fiber. Not every region supports zones, and spreading across them can cost extra for duplication and data transfer.

cards.front: What extra advantages do region pairs give?
cards.back: In a large outage one region of each pair is prioritized for recovery. Planned updates roll out to paired regions one at a time. Data stays inside the same geography for residency and compliance (except Brazil South).

cards.front: Which regions are exceptions to normal region pairing?
cards.back: Brazil South pairs one-way with South Central US, outside its geography. Italy North, Poland Central and Israel Central have no traditional pair and rely on availability zones plus geo-redundant storage. Not every service fails over automatically: some recovery must be configured by you.

cards.front: Azure DNS: what are its main benefits?
cards.back: Reliability from anycast (the closest DNS server answers), security through Azure Resource Manager (RBAC, activity logs, resource locks), ease of use (portal, CLI, PowerShell, API, same billing), private DNS domains for your VNets, and alias records.

cards.front: What is an alias record in Azure DNS?
cards.back: A record set that points to an Azure resource (public IP, Traffic Manager profile or CDN endpoint). If the resource IP changes, the alias updates itself during resolution.

cards.front: Can you buy a domain name with Azure DNS?
cards.back: No. Buy it from App Service domains or a third-party registrar (annual fee), then host the domain in Azure DNS to manage its records.

cards.front: What does Microsoft Entra ID provide?
cards.back: Authentication (self-service password reset, MFA, banned password lists, smart lockout), single sign-on, application management (Application Proxy, SaaS integration, My Apps) and device management (Intune, device-based Conditional Access). Connected to on-premises AD it can also flag suspicious sign-ins at no extra cost.

cards.front: How does Microsoft Entra Domain Services work?
cards.back: You pick a namespace and Azure deploys two Windows Server domain controllers (a replica set) that Microsoft manages. Gives domain join, group policy, LDAP and Kerberos/NTLM without running DCs yourself, ideal for lifting legacy apps. Sync is ONE-WAY from Entra ID to the managed domain.

cards.front: Microsoft Entra Connect: what does it do?
cards.back: Synchronizes identities between on-premises Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID so users get one consistent experience (SSO, MFA, self-service password reset) on premises and in the cloud, instead of maintaining two identity sets.

cards.front: Zero Trust: the three principles and their actions?
cards.back: Verify explicitly (authenticate and authorize on all data points). Use least privilege access (just-in-time and just-enough-access, risk-based adaptive policies). Assume breach (segment access, verify end-to-end encryption, use analytics for threat detection). Access depends on authentication, not network location.

cards.front: Defense in depth: name the seven layers, outermost to innermost.
cards.back: Physical, Identity and access, Perimeter (DDoS protection, perimeter firewalls), Network (segmentation, deny by default), Compute (secure VM access, patching, endpoint protection), Application (secure code, secrets in Key Vault), Data (encryption at rest and in transit).

cards.front: Azure Key Vault: what does it hold and why use it?
cards.back: Secrets (connection strings, passwords), encryption keys and certificates. Gives access control, key rotation and usage auditing, and lets apps fetch secrets at runtime with managed identities instead of hard-coded credentials. Can separate duties for who views, uses and rotates keys.

cards.front: Defender for Cloud: assess, secure, defend?
cards.back: Continuously assess (vulnerability assessment, track posture). Secure (harden with the Microsoft cloud security benchmark, recommendations grouped into controls with a secure score, built on Azure Policy). Defend (security alerts, kill-chain correlation, advanced threat protection such as just-in-time VM access).

cards.front: Where does Defender for Cloud protect?
cards.back: Azure PaaS and data services, networks, on-premises servers (deploy Azure Arc and enable enhanced security), and other clouds (AWS EC2 and EKS, GCP). One control plane for hybrid and multicloud.

questions.q: A hospital must keep patient records in its own datacenter but wants to run public-facing apps with extra capacity during flu season. Which model fits?
questions.why: Hybrid combines on-premises or private resources with public cloud capacity. Sensitive data stays private while peaks use the public cloud.

questions.q: Which TWO describe a private cloud?
opts: You purchase and maintain the hardware
You pay only for the capacity you use
You control the physical resources and security
Resources are provisioned instantly from shared capacity
questions.why: Hardware purchase (CapEx) and control of resources and security are private cloud traits. Pay-for-use and instant shared provisioning describe the public cloud.

questions.q: Buying servers for a new datacenter is an example of which expense type?
questions.why: One-time upfront spending on hardware is capital expenditure. Operational expenditure is billed as you go.

questions.q: A startup wants no upfront infrastructure cost and a bill that drops when it uses less. Which model fits?
questions.why: Consumption-based billing means you pay only for what you use, so cost follows demand.

questions.q: A company will run the same VMs at steady usage for three years. Which pricing approach is usually cheapest?
questions.why: Predictable, steady usage is what commitment-based pricing rewards with a lower unit price.

questions.q: In every cloud service type, which item stays the customer's responsibility?
questions.why: Customers always own their data, devices and accounts. Microsoft always owns the physical datacenter, network and hosts.

questions.q: You run an app on an Azure virtual machine. Who patches the guest operating system?
questions.why: A VM is IaaS, so you manage the OS and everything above it.

questions.q: Developers want to ship a web app without managing servers or the OS. Which service type?
questions.why: PaaS handles the platform so developers focus on their app and data.

questions.q: Which of these is a PaaS offering?
questions.why: Cosmos DB is a managed database platform (PaaS). VMs and virtual networks are IaaS; Microsoft 365 is SaaS.

questions.q: Which service type is usually licensed by monthly or annual subscription?
questions.why: SaaS is finished software hosted for you and billed by subscription.

questions.q: An app adds extra virtual machines when traffic rises. What is this?
questions.why: Adding instances is scaling out (horizontal). Scaling up adds CPU or RAM to one instance.

questions.q: An app shrinks back to two instances at night and grows to ten at lunchtime, automatically. This is an example of:
questions.why: Elasticity means resources scale automatically with demand, in both directions.

questions.q: Which benefit do you gain by spreading resources across multiple Azure regions?
questions.why: Multiple regions keep the service running if one region has an outage.

questions.q: Cloud-based backup, replication and geo-distribution are all part of a:
questions.why: These services keep data and code safe if a disaster hits one site.

questions.q: Two services in a chain have SLAs of 99.9% and 99.95%. The composite SLA is closest to:
questions.why: Multiply: 0.999 × 0.9995 ≈ 0.9985, so about 99.85%. It is always lower than the weakest link.

questions.q: Which TWO are cloud benefits listed for reliability and predictability?
questions.why: Reliability: resiliency, redundancy, failover. Predictability: performance and cost.

questions.q: Physically separate datacenters inside one Azure region, each with independent power, cooling and networking, are called:
questions.why: Availability zones sit inside a region. Region pairs link two regions.

questions.q: A region pair always sits within the same:
questions.why: Pairs are in the same geography and at least 300 miles apart.

questions.q: A storage account is an example of a:
questions.why: A resource is a manageable item. Resource groups hold resources.

questions.q: Which can you use to apply policy and access control across multiple subscriptions?
questions.why: Management groups sit above subscriptions. Administrative units are for Entra resources.

questions.q: You assign a role at a resource group. Which resources does it apply to?
opts: Existing and future resources in the group
questions.why: Access applied at the group scope inherits to all current and future resources in it.

questions.q: Which service runs code only when triggered by an event and bills for execution time?
questions.why: Functions is serverless, event-driven compute.

questions.q: Which option protects VMs from planned maintenance and hardware failures within a region at no extra cost?
questions.why: An availability set spreads VMs across update and fault domains.

questions.q: You need an encrypted connection between an on-premises datacenter and an Azure virtual network over the internet. Which service?
questions.why: VPN Gateway builds encrypted tunnels over the public internet. ExpressRoute is a private line.

questions.q: Resources in two Azure virtual networks must communicate. What do you configure?
questions.why: Peering links two VNets over Microsoft's backbone.

questions.q: How can an Azure SQL database be reached from a VNet over the Azure backbone?
questions.why: Service endpoints extend your VNet identity to the Azure service. Private endpoints give it a private IP.

questions.q: Which TWO connect an on-premises network to Azure?
questions.why: VPN Gateway and ExpressRoute both link on-premises to Azure. Bastion is browser RDP/SSH; an NSG filters traffic.

questions.q: Which connection does NOT travel over the public internet?
opts: VNet peering over a public IP
questions.why: ExpressRoute is a private connection through a provider.

questions.q: Which blob tier stores data offline with the lowest storage cost and the highest access cost?
questions.why: Archive is offline and must be rehydrated before use.

questions.q: Which blob tier has the highest storage cost and fastest access?
questions.why: Hot is for frequently accessed data.

questions.q: Which TWO protocols can you use to access an Azure file share?
questions.why: Azure Files supports SMB and NFS.

questions.q: Which TWO are common uses of Blob storage?
opts: Serving images directly to a browser
Mounting a shared drive on many VMs
questions.why: Blob handles unstructured data and backups. Azure Files is the mountable share and Disk storage backs VMs.

questions.q: Which redundancy option protects against a whole-region outage?
questions.why: GRS (and GZRS) copy data to a second region.

questions.q: Which service gives you managed Active Directory features such as domain join and Group Policy without deploying domain controllers?
questions.why: Domain Services provides managed AD DS. Connect syncs on-premises AD to Entra ID.

questions.q: A user signs in once and can open many apps without signing in again. This is:
questions.why: SSO reuses one sign-in across apps.

questions.q: Access is allowed only if the user is on a compliant device, otherwise MFA is required. Which feature?
questions.why: Conditional Access evaluates signals and then allows, blocks or requires more proof.

questions.q: Which TWO are passwordless methods?
questions.why: FIDO2 keys, Windows Hello for Business and Authenticator are passwordless options.

questions.q: Which Azure service stores secrets, keys and certificates securely?
questions.why: Key Vault is the central secure store.

questions.q: Which TWO can you do with Cost Management + Billing?
questions.why: Cost Management covers budgets, analysis and forecasts. The pricing calculator estimates before deployment; Policy restricts regions.

questions.q: You need to estimate the cost of a planned deployment before creating any resources. What do you use?
questions.why: The pricing calculator estimates cost from the services and usage you choose.

questions.q: You want to group costs by department across resources. Which feature helps?
questions.why: Tags are name-value pairs used to organize and track cost.

questions.q: Which service stops people from deploying resources outside approved regions?
questions.why: Azure Policy enforces rules such as allowed locations.

questions.q: Which feature prevents anyone, even an Owner, from accidentally deleting a resource group?
questions.why: A CanNotDelete lock blocks deletion until the lock is removed.

questions.q: What controls WHAT a user can do, rather than what a resource may be?
questions.why: RBAC grants permissions to users. Policy governs resource configuration.

questions.q: Which TWO actions can you take in the Azure portal?
opts: Move a VM to another region by dragging it
Change a VM's availability zone in place
questions.why: The portal can create resources and Entra users. Zone placement is fixed at creation.

questions.q: Which management layer receives requests from any Azure tool and creates, updates or deletes resources?
questions.why: Every tool goes through ARM.

questions.q: You need to manage on-premises servers with Azure governance and security without migrating them. What do you use?
questions.why: Azure Arc projects non-Azure servers into Azure for management.

questions.q: Which TWO can create a virtual machine from a phone's browser?
questions.why: Both run in a browser. Cloud Shell offers Bash and PowerShell.

questions.q: Which service recommends changes to improve reliability, security, performance and cost?
questions.why: Advisor evaluates your resources and gives recommendations.

questions.q: Which service notifies you of an Azure outage or planned maintenance in your region?
questions.why: Service Health reports service issues and planned maintenance that affect you.

questions.q: Which service can alert you when CPU stays above 80% for five minutes and trigger autoscale?
questions.why: Azure Monitor collects metrics and drives alerts and autoscale.

questions.q: A batch rendering job can restart if interrupted and must cost as little as possible. Which pricing option fits?
questions.why: Spot uses unused capacity at a lower price, but Azure can evict the VM. That suits interruptible work.

questions.q: Your compute spend is steady, but workloads move between VM families and services. Which option gives a discount without tying you to one VM type?
opts: Azure Reservation for one VM size
questions.why: A savings plan commits you to an hourly spend, not a specific VM type.

questions.q: Which TWO are alert types in Cost Management?
questions.why: Cost Management has budget, credit and department spending quota alerts.

questions.q: You tag a resource group with Environment=Prod. What happens to resources already inside it?
opts: They inherit it only after a restart
They inherit it only if a lock is set
questions.why: Resources don't inherit tags from resource groups or subscriptions. Policy can add or require tags.

questions.q: A subscription Owner needs to change a resource that has a ReadOnly lock. What must happen first?
opts: Move the resource to another subscription
questions.why: Locks apply regardless of RBAC permissions, so remove the lock before the change.

questions.q: Which service provides automated data discovery, sensitive data classification and end-to-end lineage?
questions.why: Purview is Microsoft's data governance, risk and compliance solution.

questions.q: Where can you find Microsoft's audit reports and compliance documentation?
questions.why: The Service Trust Portal provides security, privacy and compliance content.

questions.q: You want to know whether a specific VM has a problem and whether it is on Azure's side or yours. Which view?
questions.why: Resource Health covers individual resources. Service Health covers the services and regions you use; Azure Status is global.

questions.q: Which TWO can Azure Arc manage outside Azure?
opts: Azure Virtual Desktop host pools in Azure
questions.why: Arc covers servers, Kubernetes clusters, Azure data services, SQL Server and (preview) VMs.

questions.q: Which is a declarative language, simpler than JSON ARM templates, for deploying Azure resources?
questions.why: Bicep is declarative and deploys through ARM.

questions.q: What decides who is notified, and what happens, when an Azure Monitor alert fires?
questions.why: An alert rule defines the condition; an action group defines the response.

questions.q: Which Azure Monitor feature tracks response times and failure rates of a web application?
questions.why: Application Insights monitors web app performance and usage.

questions.q: A team runs a development environment only during business hours. Which action best supports sustainability and cost efficiency?
opts: Run the VMs 24/7 so they are always ready
Automatically shut the environment down overnight and on weekends
Move the workload back on premises
questions.why: Turning off or deallocating unused resources reduces waste. Learn ties sustainability to right-sizing, automating, monitoring and optimizing.

questions.q: You want to add speech and vision features to an app through APIs without training your own model. Which should you use?
questions.why: Azure AI services provide prebuilt AI features through APIs. Azure Machine Learning is for building and training custom models.

questions.q: Your data scientists must build, train and manage a custom machine learning model. Which Azure service fits?
questions.why: Use Azure Machine Learning for custom model development, experimentation and lifecycle management.

questions.q: Which service enables secure, two-way communication between cloud services and IoT devices?
questions.why: IoT Hub is the messaging hub between the cloud and devices. IoT Edge runs workloads on the devices themselves.

questions.q: You need cloud analytics logic to run on devices close to where the data is generated. Which service extends the cloud to those devices?
questions.why: Azure IoT Edge extends cloud capabilities to edge devices so workloads run near the data.

questions.q: Which TWO workloads can Azure App Service host? Choose 2.
questions.why: App Service hosts web apps, API apps, WebJobs and mobile app back ends without you managing the infrastructure.

questions.q: Which Azure service does NOT require you to choose a region when you create it?
questions.why: Global services such as Microsoft Entra ID, Azure Traffic Manager and Azure DNS do not need a region.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of separate availability zones in an availability zone-enabled region?
questions.why: Every zone-enabled region has at least three separate zones. Not all regions support zones.

questions.q: Which TWO are advantages of Azure region pairs? Choose 2.
opts: One region of each pair is prioritized for recovery after a large outage
Planned updates are rolled out to paired regions one at a time
All data is replicated to every Azure region automatically
Paired regions are always in different geographies
questions.why: Pairs get prioritized recovery and staggered updates. Data stays in the same geography (Brazil South is the exception) and not every service replicates automatically.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of an alias record set in Azure DNS?
opts: To follow an Azure resource automatically when its IP address changes
To connect on-premises networks to Azure
questions.why: An alias record points to an Azure resource (public IP, Traffic Manager, CDN endpoint) and updates itself when the IP changes.

questions.q: You must register contoso.com and manage its records in Azure. What should you do?
opts: Buy it from App Service domains or a registrar, then host it in Azure DNS
questions.why: You cannot buy a domain with Azure DNS. Purchase elsewhere, then host the domain in Azure DNS.

questions.q: Which Microsoft Entra Domain Services statement is true?
opts: Changes sync from the managed domain back to Entra ID
Sync is one-way from Microsoft Entra ID to the managed domain
You must deploy and patch the domain controllers yourself
questions.why: A managed domain syncs one way from Entra ID. Microsoft runs the two domain controllers for you.

questions.q: Which Zero Trust principle is about just-in-time and just-enough-access?
questions.why: Least privilege access limits access with JIT/JEA and risk-based adaptive policies.

questions.q: In defense in depth, DDoS protection belongs to which layer?
questions.why: The perimeter layer uses DDoS protection to filter large-scale attacks and perimeter firewalls to alert on malicious activity.

questions.q: Storing application secrets in Azure Key Vault belongs to which defense-in-depth layer?
questions.why: The application layer keeps sensitive application secrets in secure storage such as Key Vault.

questions.q: Which TWO items can Azure Key Vault securely store? Choose 2.
questions.why: Key Vault stores secrets, encryption keys and certificates, with access control, rotation and auditing.

questions.q: Which Microsoft Defender for Cloud feature summarizes your overall security posture as a number?
questions.why: Recommendations are grouped into security controls and rolled into a secure score.

questions.q: To protect on-premises servers with Defender for Cloud, which Azure service do you deploy?
questions.why: Azure Arc extends Defender plans to non-Azure machines.

questions.q: Which three needs does Microsoft Defender for Cloud address?
questions.why: Defender for Cloud continuously assesses, helps secure (harden) and defends (alerts and threat protection).

questions.q: A company runs workloads in Azure and in another cloud provider at the same time. Which cloud model is this?
questions.why: Multi-cloud means using more than one public cloud provider. Hybrid means combining public cloud with private or on-premises resources.

questions.q: Which Azure service lets you manage servers and Kubernetes clusters in on-premises, multi-cloud and Azure environments from one place?
questions.why: Azure Arc extends Azure management to resources outside Azure, so hybrid and multi-cloud environments can be managed together.

questions.q: A company wants to run its existing VMware workloads in Azure with minimal changes. Which service fits?
questions.why: Azure VMware Solution runs VMware workloads in Azure with seamless integration and scalability.

questions.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of the consumption-based model?
opts: Pay for additional resources only when needed
Stop paying for resources you no longer need
A large upfront investment in hardware
questions.why: Consumption-based pricing means no upfront hardware purchase. You pay for what you use and stop paying when you stop using it.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Operational expenditure (OpEx) is spending on products and services as you use them.
Capital expenditure (CapEx) is typically a one-time, upfront spend on physical infrastructure.
Paying monthly for Azure resources you consume is an example of CapEx.
questions.why: Cloud consumption is OpEx: you pay as you use. CapEx is upfront spending on things like buildings and servers.

questions.q: Which item is ALWAYS the cloud provider's responsibility, whatever the service type?
questions.why: Microsoft always owns the physical layer. The customer always owns their data, devices, accounts and identities.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: With SaaS, the customer patches the operating system.
With IaaS, the customer manages the operating system.
The customer is always responsible for the information and data they store.
questions.why: In SaaS the provider manages the OS and the app. In IaaS you manage the OS. Data is always the customer's responsibility.

questions.q: What does high availability focus on?
opts: Making sure resources stay available, even when something goes wrong
questions.why: High availability is about keeping resources available with maximum uptime, as described in service-level agreements (SLAs).

questions.q: Match each example to the cloud benefit it shows.
rows: Resources are added automatically when demand rises
A workload keeps running when one datacenter fails
You forecast next month's bill with the pricing calculator
Policies make every deployment meet company standards
questions.why: Scalability adjusts resources to demand. Reliability means recovering from failures. Predictability covers performance and cost forecasting. Governance uses policies and templates to keep deployments compliant.

questions.q: Managing Azure through the portal, CLI, APIs or PowerShell is an example of which benefit?
questions.why: Management in the cloud is HOW you manage: portal, CLI, APIs, PowerShell. Management of the cloud is WHAT the cloud does for you, like autoscaling and alerts.

questions.q: Automatically scaling resources based on need and getting alerts from monitoring are examples of what?
questions.why: Management of the cloud covers managing your resources: autoscaling, templates, monitoring alerts and automatic replacement of failing resources.

questions.q: Match each scenario to the cloud service type.
rows: Lift-and-shift an on-premises server to a cloud VM
Use Microsoft 365 for company email
Deploy a web app to Azure App Service without managing the OS
questions.why: IaaS gives you VMs to manage. PaaS manages the platform so you deploy code. SaaS is a finished app you subscribe to.

questions.q: Which cloud service type leaves the customer the least management responsibility?
questions.why: With SaaS the provider manages almost everything. You manage your data, devices, and accounts and identities.

questions.q: Serverless computing, such as Azure Functions, is most like which service type?
questions.why: Like PaaS, serverless removes infrastructure management so developers focus on code.

questions.q: Which is an example of IaaS?
questions.why: Virtual machines give you control of the OS and software, which is infrastructure as a service.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of availability zones in a region that supports them?
questions.why: Each region that supports availability zones has a minimum of three separate zones.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Most regions are paired with another region in the same geography.
If a large outage affects both regions in a pair, one of them is prioritized for recovery.
Planned Azure updates roll out to both regions in a pair at the same time.
questions.why: Updates roll out to one region in a pair at a time to limit downtime. Pairs sit in the same geography, and one region per pair gets recovery priority.

questions.q: A US government agency needs a physically isolated instance of Azure. Which should it use?
questions.why: Sovereign regions such as US DoD Central and US Gov Virginia are physically and logically isolated instances of Azure for government agencies and partners.

questions.q: Which Azure services are always available from Azure geographies and are resilient to zone-wide and region-wide outages?
questions.why: Non-regional services are always available from Azure geographies. Zonal services pin to one zone; zone-redundant services replicate across zones.

questions.q: Match each description to the Azure organizing structure.
rows: A single VM or storage account
A logical container that can't be nested
A unit of billing and an access boundary
Groups subscriptions so policy and access apply at scale
questions.why: Resources live in resource groups, resource groups live in subscriptions, and management groups organize subscriptions.

questions.q: How many levels of depth can a management group tree support, not counting the root level or the subscription level?
questions.why: A management group tree supports up to six levels of depth. One directory can hold up to 10,000 management groups.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: A resource can belong to two resource groups at the same time.
Deleting a resource group deletes every resource inside it.
Resource groups can be nested inside other resource groups.
questions.why: Each resource is in exactly one resource group, groups can't be nested, and deleting a group deletes everything in it.

questions.q: Which feature spreads VMs across racks with separate power and networking, so one rack failure doesn't take them all down?
opts: Fault domains in an availability set
Update domains in an availability set
questions.why: Fault domains group VMs by common power source and network switch. Update domains group VMs that can be rebooted together during maintenance.

questions.q: You need to centrally manage and update a large number of identical, load-balanced VMs that scale with demand. What should you use?
questions.why: Virtual machine scale sets create and manage a group of identical, load-balanced VMs and can scale automatically.

questions.q: Which service provides desktop and app virtualization in the cloud, including multi-session Windows?
questions.why: Azure Virtual Desktop delivers a full Windows desktop and apps from the cloud to almost any device.

questions.q: You want to run a single container quickly without managing VMs or an orchestrator. Which service fits?
questions.why: Azure Container Instances is the fastest, simplest way to run a container in Azure as a PaaS offering.

questions.q: Match each need to the compute service.
rows: Event-driven code that runs only when triggered
Host a web app or REST API without managing servers
Full control of the operating system
Orchestrate many containerized microservices
questions.why: Functions is event-driven serverless code. App Service hosts web apps and APIs. VMs give OS control. AKS orchestrates containers.

questions.q: Which kind of VPN gateway is the preferred connection method for on-premises devices?
questions.why: Route-based VPN gateways use routes in the IP forwarding table to direct packets and are the preferred, more resilient option.

questions.q: Two Azure virtual networks must talk to each other directly, with traffic staying on the Microsoft backbone. What should you configure?
questions.why: Virtual network peering connects VNets directly. Traffic between peered networks is private and stays on the Microsoft backbone.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Azure DNS can host your DNS domains and manage their records.
You can buy a domain name through Azure DNS.
Azure DNS supports private DNS zones for names inside virtual networks.
questions.why: Azure DNS hosts domains and supports private zones, but you can't buy a domain name with Azure DNS. You buy it from a registrar.

questions.q: An Azure resource must be reachable only from inside your virtual network, not from the internet. What should you use?
questions.why: A private endpoint gives the resource a private IP address in your VNet, so it isn't exposed on the public internet.

questions.q: Match each redundancy option to its description.
rows: Three copies in one datacenter
Three copies across three availability zones in one region
Locally redundant copies plus copies in a secondary region
Zone-redundant copies plus copies in a secondary region
questions.why: LRS is one datacenter. ZRS spreads across zones. GRS adds a secondary region to LRS. GZRS adds a secondary region to ZRS.

questions.q: Data is rarely accessed but must be stored at least 90 days and still be readable in milliseconds, at lower cost than the cool tier. Which tier?
questions.why: The cold tier is online with fast retrieval, costs less to store than cool, and has a 90-day minimum. Archive is offline.

questions.q: Which statement about the archive access tier is true?
opts: Data is offline and must be rehydrated before it can be read
Data can be read in milliseconds
It has no minimum storage duration
It has the highest storage cost
questions.why: Archive is offline with the lowest storage cost. Data must be rehydrated (hours) and should stay at least 180 days.

questions.q: Which service offers fully managed file shares that can be mounted over SMB or NFS?
questions.why: Azure Files provides fully managed file shares accessible over SMB and NFS.

questions.q: You must move a very large amount of data to Azure, and your network connection is too slow. What should you use?
questions.why: Azure Data Box is a physical device shipped to you to move large amounts of data offline.

questions.q: Which command-line utility copies blobs or files to or from a storage account?
questions.why: AzCopy is a command-line tool for copying blobs or files to or from your storage account.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: With GRS, you can read data from the secondary region at any time.
The archive tier stores data offline.
Data in the cool tier should be stored for at least 30 days.
questions.why: Plain GRS doesn't allow reads from the secondary. You need RA-GRS or RA-GZRS for that. Archive is offline. Cool has a 30-day minimum.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Zero Trust assumes a breach and verifies each request.
Zero Trust trusts devices on the corporate network by default.
Using least-privileged access is a Zero Trust principle.
questions.why: Zero Trust principles: verify explicitly, use least-privileged access, and assume breach. Nothing is trusted just because it is on the corporate network.

questions.q: Which defense-in-depth layer focuses on limiting network connectivity between resources to only what is required?
questions.why: The network layer limits communication between resources through segmentation and access controls.

questions.q: Users signing in from the office should sign in normally, but sign-ins from unknown locations must use MFA. What enforces this?
questions.why: Conditional Access uses signals such as user, location and device to allow access, require MFA or block it.

questions.q: Which TWO are passwordless authentication methods?
questions.why: Passwordless options include Windows Hello for Business, the Microsoft Authenticator app and FIDO2 security keys.

questions.q: A legacy app needs domain join, Kerberos and LDAP, but you don't want to deploy domain controllers. What should you use?
questions.why: Microsoft Entra Domain Services provides managed domain services such as domain join, Group Policy, LDAP and Kerberos without running your own domain controllers.

questions.q: Partner users must sign in to your apps with their own credentials. Which capability supports this?
questions.why: External identities let people outside your organization use their own identity to access your apps and resources.

questions.q: Match each need to the tool.
rows: Estimate the monthly cost of new Azure services
Compare on-premises costs with running in Azure
Track actual spending and set budgets
Get recommendations such as shutting down underused VMs
questions.why: The pricing calculator estimates new Azure costs. The TCO calculator compares on-premises with Azure. Cost Management tracks real spend and budgets. Advisor recommends savings.

questions.q: Which network traffic is generally free?
opts: Inbound data transfers into Azure datacenters
Outbound data transfers out of Azure datacenters
questions.why: Some inbound data transfers, such as data going into Azure datacenters, are free. Outbound transfers are usually charged.

questions.q: Which Cost Management alert tells you when spending reaches a threshold you set?
questions.why: Budget alerts fire when spending, based on usage or cost, reaches or exceeds the amount in the budget alert condition.

questions.q: You want to group resources by cost center so billing reports can be broken down by team. What should you use?
questions.why: Tags are name-value pairs such as CostCenter=Finance. They help organize resources and report costs by team or project.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: The same resource can cost different amounts in different regions.
Third-party solutions from Azure Marketplace can add to your bill.
Reserved instances increase the cost of steady, predictable workloads.
questions.why: Geography affects price, Marketplace solutions can add charges, and reservations lower costs for steady workloads when you commit for one or three years.

questions.q: You want to stop a resource from being deleted but still allow changes to it. Which lock?
questions.why: A Delete lock allows reads and changes but blocks deletion. A ReadOnly lock blocks both changes and deletion.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: A ReadOnly lock prevents both changes and deletion.
Resource locks apply even to users with the Owner role.
Once a resource lock is applied, it can never be removed.
questions.why: Locks apply to everyone, including Owners. To delete or change the resource you first remove the lock, which takes a deliberate extra step.

questions.q: In Azure Policy, what is a group of related policy definitions tracked together toward one goal?
questions.why: An initiative groups related policies so you can assign and track them together, for example to meet a security standard.

questions.q: Which service helps you discover, classify and govern data across on-premises, multicloud and SaaS sources?
questions.why: Microsoft Purview is a family of data governance, risk and compliance solutions for a unified view of your data.

questions.q: Where can you get Microsoft's compliance and audit reports, such as ISO and SOC reports?
questions.why: The Service Trust Portal gives access to Microsoft's security, privacy and compliance reports and documents.

questions.q: Match each need to the tool.
rows: A browser-based shell with Bash or PowerShell and nothing to install
Declarative JSON files for repeatable deployments
A language that compiles to ARM JSON with simpler syntax
Manage on-premises and other-cloud servers as if they were in Azure
questions.why: Cloud Shell runs in the browser. ARM templates are declarative JSON. Bicep is a simpler language for the same deployments. Arc extends Azure management beyond Azure.

sections.title: Cloud computing
sections.label: High
sections.note: Shared responsibility and cloud models appear on almost every attempt.
obj: public, private, hybrid and use cases
cold: **Cloud computing**: services (servers, storage, databases, networking, software) over the internet, on demand.
**Public**: provider-owned, shared hardware, no upfront hardware cost. **Private**: one organization, you manage hardware. **Hybrid**: both, workloads move between.

**Shared responsibility**: Microsoft always owns physical datacenter, network, hosts. You always own data, devices, accounts and identities. OS, network controls, applications and identity infrastructure vary by service type.
**CapEx** = upfront spend on hardware. **OpEx** = pay as you go. Consumption-based = pay only for what you use.
**Use cases:** public = variable load and test/dev; private = strict compliance or control; hybrid = sensitive data on-premises plus public capacity.

**Pricing models:** pay-as-you-go (flexible), Reservations and savings plans (commit 1 or 3 years, cheaper if steady), Spot (interruptible, lowest price). Azure Hybrid Benefit reuses existing licenses.
**Serverless**: you run code, the provider manages servers and scales automatically (Azure Functions).
traps: Which model buys hardware: private. Which is pay-as-you-go: public.
"Who patches the OS?" depends on IaaS (you) vs PaaS/SaaS (Microsoft).
Hybrid is not "multiple public clouds".
hooks: Public = shared. Private = yours. Hybrid = both.
CapEx = buy it. OpEx = rent it.

sections.label: High
sections.note: Includes the SLA math you've missed in practice.
cold: **Scale up (vertical)** = bigger resource. **Scale out (horizontal)** = more instances.
**Scalability** = add or remove resources for load. **Elasticity** = do it automatically with demand.
**Reliability** = resiliency, redundancy, failover. **Predictability** = performance (autoscale, load balance, HA) and cost.
**Composite SLA = multiply** the SLAs; result is lower than any single one.
Downtime per year: 99% ≈ 3.65 days · 99.9% ≈ 8.76 hrs · 99.99% ≈ 52.6 min.
Management **of** the cloud (autoscale, templates, monitoring) vs management **in** the cloud (portal, CLI, PowerShell, APIs).
traps: Scalability vs elasticity (weak area).
Adding a component to a chain lowers the composite SLA.
hooks: Up = bigger box. Out = more boxes.
Composite SLA = multiply.

sections.label: High
sections.note: IaaS shared responsibility is a current weak area.
obj: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and their use cases.
cold: **IaaS**: rent VMs, storage, networks. You manage OS, apps, data. Lift and shift, test/dev.
**PaaS**: build and deploy apps without managing servers or OS. You manage app and data.
**SaaS**: finished software, usually subscription (Microsoft 365). You manage data and access.
Moving IaaS → PaaS → SaaS, Microsoft manages more.

App Service, Functions are PaaS/serverless.

obj: Azure regions, region pairs, sovereign regions
The hierarchy of resource groups, subscriptions and management groups
cold: Geography → region → availability zone → datacenter
Region pair = same geography, at least 300 miles apart; Brazil South is the one-way exception
Zonal vs zone-redundant vs non-regional services
Hierarchy: Tenant Root Group → management groups → subscriptions → resource groups → resources
Resource group rules: one group per resource, no nesting, no renaming, delete group = delete contents
Subscription = billing boundary + access control boundary
Management groups: 6 levels deep, 10,000 per directory, one parent

Thinking a resource can be in two resource groups
Forgetting that group settings apply to current and future resources (module quiz miss)

300 miles = a pair; zones are neighbors
A group is a box: trash the box, trash the contents

Application hosting: web apps, containers, virtual machines

Scale set = identical VMs that auto scale; availability set = update and fault domains inside one region
VM name decoder: Standard_D2s_v5
Container Instances vs Container Apps vs AKS
Functions: event-driven, serverless, pay only while running; Durable Functions = stateful
App Service types: web apps, API apps, WebJobs, mobile apps
AI services (prebuilt) vs Machine Learning (custom) vs IoT

Update domain (planned reboots) vs fault domain (shared power or network)
Picking a VM when the scenario says 'no infrastructure to manage'

Event in, code runs, pay only while it runs

sections.title: Networking
sections.label: Medium-High
sections.note: 2 official objectives (virtual networking; public and private endpoints), but they cover a lot of ground
sections.why: Fewer objective lines than other sections, but each one is a service you must tell apart. The VPN vs ExpressRoute comparison is a classic exam question.
obj: Virtual networking: virtual networks, subnets, peering, Azure DNS, VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute
cold: VNet = private IP space split into subnets; NSGs filter, route tables and UDRs route
Peering joins VNets privately over the Microsoft backbone, even across regions
VPN Gateway: encrypted over the internet; site-to-site, point-to-site, network-to-network
VPN HA: active/standby, active/active, ExpressRoute failover, zone-redundant
ExpressRoute: private circuit through a provider, no public internet; DNS, certificate checks and CDN still use the internet
Azure DNS: anycast, Resource Manager (RBAC, logs, locks), private zones, alias records
Public endpoint = public IP; private endpoint = private IP inside the VNet
traps: VPN vs ExpressRoute: encrypted-over-internet vs private line
Point-to-site is one device, site-to-site is a building
Assuming ExpressRoute sends absolutely everything privately (DNS and CDN still go over the internet)
hooks: Subnets slice it, NSGs guard it, peering joins it
Site = building, Point = person, Network = VNet
ExpressRoute = your own private road

sections.note: 6 official objectives

obj: Describe storage account options and storage types
Options for moving files: AzCopy, Azure Storage Explorer, Azure File Sync
Migration options: Azure Migrate and Azure Data Box
cold: Five services: Blobs, Files, Queues, Disks, Tables
Tiers: hot, cool (30 days), cold (90 days), archive (180 days); account level has no archive
Storage account names: 3-24 characters, lowercase and numbers, unique in Azure
Account types: standard general-purpose v2, premium block blobs, premium file shares, premium page blobs
LRS 11 nines, ZRS 12 nines, GRS and GZRS 16 nines; RA = read access to the secondary
AzCopy one-way, Storage Explorer graphical, File Sync two-way
Azure Migrate (whole move) vs Data Box (up to 80 TB, shipped)

Thinking the secondary region is readable by default (needs RA-GRS or RA-GZRS)
Mixing AzCopy (one-way) with File Sync (two-way)
hooks: BFQDT = Blobs, Files, Queues, Disks, Tables
30 / 90 / 180: the longer it sleeps, the cheaper the bed
Z = zones, G = geo, RA = read access
Migrate = the whole move, Data Box = a truck for the data

sections.title: Identity, access and security
sections.label: High
sections.note: 8 official objectives (the longest list in Domain 2
sections.why: The longest objective list in Domain 2, and the foundation of your whole security track: SC-900 and SC-500 build directly on these ideas. Time spent here pays off beyond AZ-900.
obj: Directory services: Microsoft Entra ID and Entra Domain Services
cold: Entra ID = cloud identity; Entra Connect syncs on-prem AD; Domain Services = managed domain for legacy apps
SSO is only as secure as the first sign-in; MFA = know, have, are
Passwordless: Windows Hello for Business, Microsoft Authenticator, FIDO2 keys
B2B collaboration (guests in your directory) vs B2B direct connect (not in your directory) vs External ID for customers
Conditional Access: signals → decision → enforcement
RBAC: role + scope, inherits downward, enforced through Resource Manager, allow model
Zero Trust: verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach
Defense in depth: 7 layers, data at the center
Key Vault stores secrets, keys and certificates; Defender for Cloud: assess, secure, defend
traps: Entra ID vs Entra Domain Services
RBAC (what you can do) vs Conditional Access (whether you get in)
Forgetting RBAC does not enforce permissions inside an application or at the data level
hooks: Passwordless = high security AND high convenience
Signal → Decision → Enforcement
Never trust, always verify
Pat Is Proud Never Cooking Any Dinner = Physical, Identity, Perimeter, Network, Compute, Application, Data
Assess, Secure, Defend
