sections.title: Cost management
sections.label: High
sections.note: You missed all three cost questions on practice test 1.
cold: **Six cost factors:** resource type, consumption, maintenance, geography, subscription type, Azure Marketplace.
**Billing zones** group regions for data-transfer pricing (not availability zones). Some inbound is free; outbound is priced by zone.
**Pricing calculator:** estimate before you deploy. Nothing is provisioned or charged. TCO calculator is retired.
**Cost Management:** cost analysis, cost alerts, budgets. Alerts: budget, credit (90% and 100%), department spending quota (EA). Budgets can trigger automation that suspends or changes resources.
**Tags:** name-value metadata for resource, cost, operations, security, governance and automation use. NOT inherited. Policy can require or reapply them.
**Pricing options:** pay-as-you-go (flexible), Reservations (stable, 1 or 3 years), savings plan for compute (hourly spend, flexible across compute), Spot (interruptible, can be evicted).
traps: Cost Management does not estimate before deployment. The pricing calculator does.
Tags do not flow down from resource groups.
Reservation is tied to specific resources; savings plan is tied to spend.
hooks: "Calculator = before. Cost Management = after."
"Reserve it, plan it, or spot it."
sections.modTitle: Describe cost management in Azure

sections.title: Governance and compliance
sections.label: High
sections.note: ## Objectives
cold: **Purview:** data governance, risk and compliance. Automated discovery, sensitive-data classification, end-to-end lineage across on-premises, multicloud and SaaS.

**Azure Policy:** create, assign and manage rules that audit or enforce configuration (allowed regions, VM sizes, required tags). Inherited downward. Evaluates new and existing resources. Can remediate. Groups of policies are initiatives.
**Resource locks:** Delete and ReadOnly. Inherited. Apply regardless of RBAC. Remove the lock first to make a change.
**Service Trust Portal:** Microsoft's security, privacy and compliance documents and audit reports. Sign in with an Entra work or school account; NDA for some content.
traps: Policy controls what resources can be. RBAC controls what users can do. Locks stop accidental change or deletion.
An Owner is still blocked by a lock.
hooks: "Policy = rules. Lock = brake. RBAC = keys."
sections.modTitle: Describe features and tools for governance and compliance

sections.title: Managing and deploying resources
sections.label: High
sections.note: ## Objectives
obj: Azure Resource Manager and ARM templates (plus Bicep, IaC).
cold: **Portal:** web GUI; dashboards; resilient, presence in every datacenter.
**Cloud Shell:** browser-based, no install, already authenticated; choose PowerShell or CLI (Bash).
**PowerShell vs CLI:** equivalent; cmdlets vs Bash-style commands; both scriptable.
**Arc:** extends Azure management and governance to servers, Kubernetes, data services, SQL Server, VMs outside Azure, through ARM.

**ARM:** every request from any tool goes through it (authenticate, authorize, send to service). ARM templates are declarative JSON: repeatable, orchestrated, modular. Bicep is a simpler declarative language.
**Copilot in Azure:** AI assistant; validate its output.
traps: Arc manages non-Azure resources without migrating them. Advisor does not.
"Create a VM from a phone" means portal or Cloud Shell.
ARM is a management layer, not a tool you install.
hooks: "Everything goes through ARM."
"Arc brings outside things in."
sections.modTitle: Describe features and tools for managing and deploying Azure resources

sections.title: Monitoring tools
sections.label: High
sections.note: Advisor, Service Health and Monitor are easy to mix up.
obj: Azure Monitor (Log Analytics, alerts, Application Insights).
cold: **Advisor:** recommendations in five categories: Reliability, Security, Performance, Operational Excellence, Cost.
**Service Health:** Azure Status (global), Service Health (your services and regions: outages, planned maintenance, advisories), Resource Health (one resource).
**Monitor:** collects metrics and logs; Log Analytics = queries; Alerts = rule + action group (metric or log based); Application Insights = web app performance and usage. Drives autoscale.
Action groups are reusable across Monitor, Service Health and Advisor.
traps: Outage or planned maintenance → Service Health, not Advisor.
CPU over 80% alert → Monitor.
Recommendation to cut cost → Advisor.
hooks: "Advisor advises. Service Health warns. Monitor measures."

meta.name: Microsoft Security, Compliance, and Identity Fundamentals

cards.front: Shared responsibility: what is ALWAYS the customer's job?
cards.back: Your **information and data**, your **devices** (PCs and mobile), and your **accounts and identities**. This holds for IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.

cards.front: Shared responsibility: what is ALWAYS Microsoft's job in the cloud?
cards.back: The **physical datacenter**, the **physical network** and the **physical hosts**.

cards.front: Name the seven defense-in-depth layers, outside to inside.
cards.back: **Physical, Identity and access, Perimeter, Network, Compute, Application, Data.** Each layer slows an attacker if the one before it fails.

cards.front: What is the CIA triad?
cards.back: **Confidentiality** (only the right people see it), **Integrity** (it is not altered), **Availability** (it is there when needed).

cards.front: Zero Trust: the three guiding principles?
cards.back: **Verify explicitly** (always authenticate and authorize on all data points), **use least privilege access** (just-in-time, just-enough), **assume breach** (segment, encrypt, monitor).

cards.front: Zero Trust: the six foundational pillars?
cards.back: **Identities, Devices (endpoints), Applications, Data, Infrastructure, Networks.**

cards.front: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption?
cards.back: **Symmetric:** one key encrypts and decrypts. **Asymmetric:** a public and private key pair. What one key encrypts, only the other decrypts.

cards.front: Encryption at rest, in transit, in use?
cards.back: **At rest:** stored data (disk, database). **In transit:** moving over a network (HTTPS/TLS). **In use:** data being processed in memory.

cards.front: What is hashing, and how is it different from encryption?
cards.back: Hashing turns data into a **fixed-length value** and is **one-way**: you cannot reverse it. The same input always gives the same hash. Used to store passwords and check integrity. **Salting** adds a random value so identical passwords get different hashes.

cards.front: GRC: what do the three letters cover?
cards.back: **Governance:** the rules and processes that direct the organization. **Risk management:** identify, assess and respond to threats. **Compliance:** follow the laws and regulations that apply.

cards.front: Data residency vs data sovereignty?
cards.back: **Residency:** rules about the physical place data may be stored. **Sovereignty:** data is subject to the laws of the country or region where it is collected, held or processed.

cards.front: Why is identity called the primary security perimeter?
cards.back: Cloud apps, personal devices and remote work mean the corporate network is no longer the edge. **Who** is signing in (person, service or device) is what you can check everywhere.

cards.front: The four pillars of an identity infrastructure?
cards.back: **Administration** (create and manage identities), **Authentication** (prove who you are), **Authorization** (what you may do), **Auditing** (track who did what).

cards.front: Authentication vs authorization?
cards.back: **Authentication (AuthN):** proving you are who you say you are. **Authorization (AuthZ):** deciding what an authenticated identity is allowed to access.

cards.front: What is an identity provider (IdP)?
cards.back: A service that **creates, stores and manages identities** and handles authentication, authorization and auditing for apps. With modern authentication the IdP issues a **security token** that apps trust. Microsoft Entra ID is one.

cards.front: What is single sign-on (SSO)?
cards.back: Sign in **once** and use that one credential to reach many apps and resources, without signing in again for each.

cards.front: What is a directory service? Name Microsoft's on-premises one.
cards.back: A hierarchical store of objects on a network (users, devices, groups). **Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)** is the on-premises one. It does not natively support mobile devices, SaaS apps or modern authentication.

cards.front: What is federation?
cards.back: A **trust relationship between identity providers** in different organizations or domains, so users sign in with their home identity. Trust is **not always two-way**.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Entra ID?
cards.back: Microsoft's **cloud-based identity and access management** service. Microsoft 365, Azure and Dynamics 365 tenants use it automatically. Formerly Azure Active Directory.

cards.front: The main identity types in Microsoft Entra ID?
cards.back: **Human** (workforce employees, and external guests, partners, customers), **workload** (applications, service principals, managed identities), **device**, and newer **agent identities** for AI agents.

cards.front: What is a service principal?
cards.back: The identity an **application** uses in a tenant, so it can be authenticated and given permissions. You must manage its credentials unless it is a managed identity.

cards.front: What is a managed identity? Two kinds?
cards.back: A service principal that **Azure manages for you**: no credentials to store or rotate. **System-assigned:** tied to one resource and deleted with it. **User-assigned:** standalone, can be shared by several resources.

cards.front: Device identity: registered vs joined vs hybrid joined?
cards.back: **Entra registered:** personal (BYOD) device, sign in with a personal or local account. **Entra joined:** organization-owned, sign in with a work account, cloud only. **Hybrid joined:** organization-owned, joined to on-premises AD and registered in Entra.

cards.front: What does Microsoft Entra External ID B2B collaboration do?
cards.back: Lets **guests** (partners, vendors) sign in with **their own identity** to use your apps. You manage their access, they manage their credentials.

cards.front: What is hybrid identity, and what makes it work?
cards.back: One identity for on-premises and cloud. **Microsoft Entra Connect Sync** or **Cloud Sync** synchronizes on-premises Active Directory with Microsoft Entra ID.

cards.front: Hybrid sign-in: password hash sync vs pass-through authentication vs federation?
cards.back: **Password hash sync:** a hash of the hash is stored in Entra, sign-in happens in the cloud, simplest. **Pass-through:** an on-premises agent validates the password, nothing stored in the cloud. **Federation:** Entra hands off to a separate trusted identity provider such as AD FS.

cards.front: What is multifactor authentication (MFA)? The three factor types?
cards.back: Sign-in that needs **two or more** of: something you **know** (password, PIN), something you **have** (phone, security key), something you **are** (fingerprint, face).

cards.front: Which authentication methods are passwordless in Microsoft Entra ID?
cards.back: **Windows Hello for Business**, **Microsoft Authenticator** (phone sign-in), and **passkeys (FIDO2)** security keys.

cards.front: Why is a Windows Hello PIN safer than a password?
cards.back: The PIN is **tied to that one device** and backed by its TPM chip. It is never sent to a server, so a stolen PIN is useless without the device.

cards.front: What are security defaults?
cards.back: Free, preconfigured baseline settings: **all users register for MFA**, **administrators must use MFA**, and **legacy authentication is blocked**. For organizations not using Conditional Access.

cards.front: What is self-service password reset (SSPR)?
cards.back: Users **change, reset or unlock** their own password with no help desk call, after proving identity with registered methods. Cuts help desk cost and downtime.

cards.front: Password protection: global vs custom banned password list?
cards.back: **Global:** maintained by Microsoft from real attack data, applied to everyone automatically. **Custom:** your own terms (brand, product names, locations). Both can also protect on-premises AD in a hybrid setup.

cards.front: Rank these by strength: password only, password + SMS, passwordless.
cards.back: Weakest: **password only**. Better: **password + second factor**. Best: **passwordless** (Windows Hello, Authenticator, passkey).

cards.front: Which methods can be used as a second factor in Entra MFA?
cards.back: Microsoft Authenticator, passkeys (FIDO2), Windows Hello for Business, OATH hardware or software tokens, SMS and voice call. A **password plus a security question is NOT MFA** in Entra sign-in.

cards.front: What is Conditional Access?
cards.back: Entra's policy engine: **if-then** rules that take **signals**, make a **decision**, and **enforce** it. Example: if a user signs in from outside the country, then require MFA.

cards.front: Conditional Access: name common signals.
cards.back: **User or group**, **location** (IP range, country), **device** (platform, compliance), **application**, and **real-time sign-in or user risk** from ID Protection.

cards.front: Conditional Access: what decisions can it make?
cards.back: **Block access**, or **grant access**, optionally with requirements: MFA, a compliant device, a hybrid joined device, an approved app, or a password change.

cards.front: Microsoft Entra roles vs Azure roles (Azure RBAC)?
cards.back: **Entra roles** control access to **Entra resources**: users, groups, apps, licenses (for example Global Administrator, User Administrator). **Azure roles** control access to **Azure resources** such as VMs and storage (Owner, Contributor, Reader).

cards.front: Built-in vs custom Entra roles?
cards.back: **Built-in:** fixed permission sets ready to use. **Custom:** you pick the permissions yourself, which needs a premium license. Always give the **least privileged** role that does the job.

cards.front: What is Global Secure Access?
cards.back: Microsoft's **Security Service Edge (SSE)** solution: **Microsoft Entra Internet Access** (secure access to internet and SaaS) and **Microsoft Entra Private Access** (secure access to private apps without a VPN).

cards.front: At which scopes can an Azure role be assigned?
cards.back: **Management group, subscription, resource group, or a single resource.** Access is inherited downward.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Entra ID Governance for?
cards.back: Making sure the **right people have the right access to the right resources at the right time**. Covers the identity lifecycle (join, move, leave), access lifecycle and privileged access lifecycle.

cards.front: What is entitlement management?
cards.back: Bundles the groups, apps and sites a role needs into an **access package**. Users request it, approval and **expiration** are built in. Works for guests too.

cards.front: What are access reviews?
cards.back: Scheduled checks where owners, managers or users themselves **confirm who still needs access** to groups, apps or roles. Access not confirmed can be removed automatically.

cards.front: What does Privileged Identity Management (PIM) do?
cards.back: Makes admin roles **just-in-time and time-bound**. Users are *eligible* and must **activate** the role, which can require **approval, MFA and a justification**. Everything is audited.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Entra ID Protection?
cards.back: Detects identity-based risks with Microsoft's threat signals, lets you **investigate** them in reports, and **remediates** automatically through risk-based Conditional Access.

cards.front: ID Protection: user risk vs sign-in risk?
cards.back: **Sign-in risk:** chance that this one sign-in is not the real owner (anonymous IP, atypical travel, password spray). **User risk:** chance that the identity itself is compromised (for example leaked credentials).

cards.front: How do you auto-remediate risk in ID Protection?
cards.back: Risk-based **Conditional Access**: medium or high **sign-in risk** requires MFA; high **user risk** requires a secure **password change**, or blocks access.

cards.front: What is a DDoS attack, and what does Azure DDoS Protection do?
cards.back: A flood of traffic meant to **exhaust an app's resources** so real users cannot reach it. Azure DDoS Protection detects and absorbs the attack at the Azure network edge.

cards.front: Azure DDoS Protection: the two paid tiers?
cards.back: **DDoS Network Protection** (covers a whole virtual network) and **DDoS IP Protection** (pay per protected public IP). Basic infrastructure protection for the Azure platform itself is on by default.

cards.front: What is Azure Firewall?
cards.back: A **managed, cloud-based, stateful network firewall**. Usually placed in a central hub virtual network to control traffic for all your networks. Built-in high availability, scales automatically, and filters with network rules, application (FQDN) rules and threat intelligence.

cards.front: What is Web Application Firewall (WAF)?
cards.back: Protects **web apps** from common exploits such as **SQL injection and cross-site scripting**. Works at layer 7. Runs on **Application Gateway, Azure Front Door** or Azure CDN.

cards.front: How do virtual networks give you segmentation?
cards.back: Each VNet is **isolated**: resources in different VNets cannot talk unless you connect them (peering). Inside a VNet you divide resources into **subnets**.

cards.front: What is a network security group (NSG)?
cards.back: A list of **allow and deny rules** that filters traffic to and from Azure resources in a VNet. Rules use **priority, source, destination, port and protocol**. Attached to a **subnet or a network interface**.

cards.front: NSG rules: how is priority processed?
cards.back: Lowest number first. The **first matching rule wins** and processing stops. Default rules (which you cannot delete) allow traffic inside the VNet and deny inbound from the internet.

cards.front: What is Azure Bastion?
cards.back: A managed service that gives **RDP and SSH to VMs from the Azure portal over TLS**. The VMs need **no public IP address**, so RDP/SSH ports are not exposed to the internet.

cards.front: What is Azure Key Vault?
cards.back: A secure store for **secrets** (passwords, connection strings), **keys** (encryption keys) and **certificates**. Access is controlled with Microsoft Entra authentication and logged.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud?
cards.back: A **cloud-native application protection platform (CNAPP)**. Three pillars: **DevSecOps**, **cloud security posture management (CSPM)** and **cloud workload protection (CWPP)**. Covers Azure, AWS, GCP and on-premises.

cards.front: What is cloud security posture management (CSPM)?
cards.back: Continuously **assesses your resources for misconfigurations** and gives hardening **recommendations**. Shows the result as a **secure score**.

cards.front: Foundational CSPM vs Defender CSPM?
cards.back: **Foundational CSPM is free:** recommendations, secure score, the Microsoft cloud security benchmark. **Defender CSPM is paid:** adds attack path analysis, cloud security explorer, agentless scanning and governance.

cards.front: What is the secure score in Defender for Cloud?
cards.back: One number that sums up your security posture from the recommendations. **Higher score means lower identified risk.** Fix recommendations and it goes up.

cards.front: What is the Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB)?
cards.back: Microsoft's set of **security best-practice controls** for Azure and other clouds. It is the **default standard** applied when you turn on Defender for Cloud.

cards.front: How do policies, standards and recommendations relate?
cards.back: A **security standard** (like MCSB or ISO 27001) is a set of rules built on **Azure Policy**. Resources are assessed against it. Each failed check becomes a **recommendation** telling you how to fix it.

cards.front: What does cloud workload protection add?
cards.back: Paid **Defender plans** per workload type (Servers, Containers, Storage, Databases, App Service, Key Vault and more). They detect threats and raise **security alerts**.

cards.front: What is just-in-time (JIT) VM access?
cards.back: A Defender for Servers feature that keeps management ports (RDP, SSH) **closed** and opens them **only on request, for a limited time**, to approved IPs.

cards.front: SIEM vs SOAR vs XDR?
cards.back: **SIEM:** collects and correlates logs from everywhere, raises alerts and incidents. **SOAR:** automates the response to those alerts with workflows. **XDR:** integrated detection and response across endpoints, identities, email and apps.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Sentinel?
cards.back: Microsoft's **cloud-native SIEM and SOAR** solution. Scales in the cloud, no servers to run.

cards.front: Sentinel: the four stages?
cards.back: **Collect** data at cloud scale, **Detect** threats with analytics and threat intelligence, **Investigate** incidents with AI and hunting, **Respond** rapidly with automation.

cards.front: Sentinel: what are data connectors?
cards.back: Built-in connections that **ingest data** from Microsoft services (Defender XDR, Entra ID, Microsoft 365), other clouds, and third-party products.

cards.front: Sentinel: analytics rules, incidents, hunting?
cards.back: **Analytics rules** correlate data into alerts. Related alerts are grouped into **incidents** to investigate. **Hunting** lets analysts search proactively with queries (KQL) before any alert fires.

cards.front: Sentinel: what are playbooks?
cards.back: Automated response workflows built on **Azure Logic Apps**. Triggered by alerts or incidents through automation rules. This is the SOAR part.

cards.front: Sentinel: what are workbooks?
cards.back: Interactive dashboards that **visualize and monitor** the data you have connected.

cards.front: Where do you use Microsoft Sentinel today?
cards.back: In the **Microsoft Defender portal**, where SIEM and XDR are unified. Azure portal support for Sentinel ends after March 31, 2027.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Defender XDR?
cards.back: A suite that **coordinates detection, prevention, investigation and response** across **endpoints, identities, email and applications**, and joins the signals into single incidents.

cards.front: What does Microsoft Defender for Office 365 protect?
cards.back: **Email and collaboration** (Exchange, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive) against **phishing, malicious links and attachments**. Includes Safe Links, Safe Attachments and attack simulation training.

cards.front: What does Microsoft Defender for Endpoint protect?
cards.back: **Devices**: laptops, phones, tablets, servers. Provides attack surface reduction, next-generation protection, **endpoint detection and response (EDR)** and automated investigation.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps?
cards.back: A **cloud access security broker (CASB)**. Discovers **shadow IT**, gives visibility and control over SaaS app use, and protects data in cloud apps.

cards.front: What does Microsoft Defender for Identity do?
cards.back: Uses **on-premises Active Directory signals** to detect compromised identities, lateral movement and insider actions.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management?
cards.back: Continuous **asset discovery and vulnerability assessment** with **risk-based prioritization** and remediation tracking for devices and software.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence?
cards.back: Microsoft's threat intelligence: **threat actor profiles, indicators of compromise, intel articles and vulnerability data** to help analysts understand and hunt threats.

cards.front: What is the Microsoft Defender portal?
cards.back: **security.microsoft.com**. One place for incidents and alerts, advanced hunting, Microsoft Secure Score, threat intelligence, and Microsoft Sentinel.

cards.front: What is the Service Trust Portal?
cards.back: Microsoft's public site (**servicetrust.microsoft.com**) for **audit reports, certifications, compliance guides and security assessments** that show how Microsoft cloud services protect your data.

cards.front: What kinds of documents are on the Service Trust Portal?
cards.back: Independent **audit reports** (SOC, ISO, FedRAMP), **penetration test and security assessment** results, compliance guides and white papers.

cards.front: Service Trust Portal: what is My Library?
cards.back: A place to **save (pin) documents** you use often. You can be **notified when Microsoft updates them**.

cards.front: Microsoft's six privacy principles?
cards.back: **Control, Transparency, Security, Strong legal protections, No content-based targeting, Benefits to you.**

cards.front: Privacy principle 'Control' vs 'Transparency'?
cards.back: **Control:** you are in charge of your data, with easy tools and clear choices. **Transparency:** Microsoft is open about data collection and use so you can make informed decisions.

cards.front: Privacy principle 'No content-based targeting'?
cards.back: Microsoft does **not use your email, chat, files or other personal content to target advertising** to you.

cards.front: Privacy principles 'Strong legal protections' and 'Benefits to you'?
cards.back: **Strong legal protections:** Microsoft respects local privacy laws and fights for privacy as a human right. **Benefits to you:** when data is collected, it is used to benefit you and improve your experience.

cards.front: What is the Microsoft Purview portal?
cards.back: **purview.microsoft.com**. One place for Purview's **data security, data governance, and risk and compliance** solutions.

cards.front: What is Compliance Manager?
cards.back: A Purview solution that helps you **assess and manage compliance** across your multicloud environment: prebuilt **assessments** for regulations, step-by-step **improvement actions**, and a **compliance score**.

cards.front: Compliance Manager: controls, assessments, regulations (templates), improvement actions?
cards.back: A **regulation** template (GDPR, ISO 27001) creates an **assessment**. The assessment is made of **controls**. Each control is met by **improvement actions** with guidance you carry out.

cards.front: Compliance Manager: three control types?
cards.back: **Microsoft-managed** (Microsoft implements), **your controls** (customer-managed, you implement), **shared** (both).

cards.front: What is the compliance score?
cards.back: A **risk-based** percentage showing progress on **improvement actions**. It helps you prioritize. It is **not a guarantee** of being compliant with a regulation.

cards.front: Compliance score vs secure score?
cards.back: **Compliance score:** Purview Compliance Manager, progress toward regulations and standards. **Secure score:** Microsoft Defender, strength of your security configuration.

cards.front: What does the default Compliance Manager assessment cover?
cards.back: The **data protection baseline**: key controls drawn from common regulations and standards, so every organization starts with an initial score.

cards.front: Microsoft Purview Information Protection: the four steps?
cards.back: **Know your data, protect your data, prevent data loss, govern your data.**

cards.front: Sensitive information types vs trainable classifiers?
cards.back: **Sensitive information types:** pattern-based (credit card, passport numbers). **Trainable classifiers:** AI that learns from examples to recognize kinds of content (resumes, source code, contracts).

cards.front: Content explorer vs Activity explorer?
cards.back: **Content explorer:** a current snapshot of **which items** have a sensitivity label, retention label or sensitive info type, and where they are. **Activity explorer:** the **history of what was done** to labeled content (label changed, file copied to USB, printed).

cards.front: What is a sensitivity label? What can it do?
cards.back: A tag you apply to documents and emails. It is **customizable, stored as clear-text metadata, and persistent** (it travels with the content). It can **encrypt**, add **markings** (header, footer, watermark), and protect containers like Teams and sites. **One sensitivity label per item.**

cards.front: What is a sensitivity label policy?
cards.back: How labels are **published** to users and groups. Can set a **default label**, require **justification to lower** a label, and make **labeling mandatory**.

cards.front: What is data loss prevention (DLP)?
cards.back: Policies that **detect and stop inappropriate sharing of sensitive information** across Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams and devices (Endpoint DLP). Actions: block, show a **policy tip**, alert.

cards.front: Retention policy vs retention label?
cards.back: **Retention policy:** the same settings for a whole location (site, mailbox). **Retention label:** set per item (document, email, folder). An item can have **only one retention label** at a time.

cards.front: What is records management?
cards.back: Declaring items as **records**: they get restrictions (cannot be deleted, edits limited), activities are logged, and at the end there is **disposition review** and proof of disposition.

cards.front: What can retention settings do?
cards.back: **Retain only**, **delete only**, or **retain then delete**. Labels can be published for users to apply or applied automatically.

cards.front: What is Insider Risk Management?
cards.back: A Purview solution to **detect, investigate and act on risky activity by people inside** the organization: data theft by departing employees, data leaks, security policy violations.

cards.front: Insider Risk Management workflow?
cards.back: **Policies** define risk indicators, **alerts** are raised, then **triage**, **investigate** in a case, and take **action** (reminder notice, or escalate).

cards.front: How does Insider Risk Management protect privacy?
cards.back: **Privacy by design:** usernames are **pseudonymized by default**, access is role-based, and investigator actions are audited.

cards.front: What is eDiscovery?
cards.back: Identifying and delivering **electronic information as evidence in legal cases**. Purview eDiscovery searches mailboxes, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive.

cards.front: eDiscovery: cases, holds, search, export?
cards.back: A **case** groups everything for one investigation. A **hold** preserves content so it cannot be deleted. **Search** finds content. **Export** delivers it. Premium features add review sets and analytics.

cards.front: Microsoft Purview Audit (Standard)?
cards.back: **On by default.** Records user and admin activity across Microsoft 365 in the unified audit log. Records are kept **180 days**.

cards.front: Microsoft Purview Audit (Premium)?
cards.back: Adds **longer retention** (one year by default for Entra ID, Exchange, SharePoint and OneDrive, **up to 10 years** with an add-on), **audit log retention policies**, and **intelligent insights** for investigations.

cards.front: Hold vs retention policy?
cards.back: An **eDiscovery hold** preserves content tied to a legal **case**. A **retention policy** governs content lifetime for compliance generally.

questions.q: A company moves its email to a SaaS service. Which is still the company's responsibility?
opts: The accounts and identities used to sign in
Patching the mail server operating system
questions.why: Customers always keep responsibility for data, devices, and accounts and identities, even in SaaS.

questions.q: A file's contents were changed by an attacker without anyone noticing. Which part of the CIA triad was broken?
questions.why: Integrity means data is not altered without authorization. Confidentiality is about who can see it, availability about access when needed.

questions.q: Which Zero Trust principle is met by limiting admins to just-in-time and just-enough access?
questions.why: Least privilege limits access with JIT and JEA. Verify explicitly is about authenticating on all signals. Assume breach is about segmenting and monitoring.

questions.q: You need to store user passwords so that the original password cannot be recovered from the stored value. What should you use?
questions.why: Hashing is one-way. Encryption can be reversed with the key, so it does not meet the requirement.

questions.q: Which defense-in-depth layer do DDoS protection and firewalls at the edge of the network belong to?
questions.why: The perimeter layer guards against network-based attacks from outside, such as DDoS. The network layer is about segmentation inside.

questions.q: Which TWO are Zero Trust guiding principles?
questions.why: The three principles are verify explicitly, use least privilege access and assume breach. Zero Trust never trusts a network location by itself.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: In asymmetric encryption, data encrypted with the public key can be decrypted with the same public key.
A hash value can be decrypted to get the original data back.
HTTPS is an example of encryption in transit.
questions.why: Asymmetric encryption needs the other key of the pair. Hashing is one-way. HTTPS (TLS) protects data moving across a network.

questions.q: Match each example to the defense-in-depth layer.
rows: Badge access to the datacenter building
Multifactor authentication for sign-in
Patching virtual machine operating systems
Encrypting a database
questions.why: Physical is the building. Identity and access controls who signs in. Compute covers VMs and endpoints. Data is the innermost layer.

questions.q: A user enters a password and then approves a prompt on their phone. Which process is this?
questions.why: Proving who you are is authentication. Authorization happens afterwards and decides what you can access.

questions.q: After sign-in, a user can read a SharePoint site but cannot edit it. Which process decided that?
questions.why: Authorization sets the level of access an authenticated identity gets.

questions.q: Users at Contoso sign in to a partner's app with their Contoso accounts. The partner's identity provider trusts Contoso's. What is this called?
questions.why: Federation is a trust relationship between identity providers across organizations.

questions.q: Which statement about Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is true?
opts: It is an on-premises directory service that does not natively support SaaS apps and modern authentication
It replaces the need for any authentication
It is the cloud identity provider included with Microsoft 365
questions.why: AD DS is the on-premises directory. Microsoft Entra ID is the cloud identity provider built for modern authentication.

questions.q: With modern authentication, what does the identity provider give the client after a successful sign-in?
opts: An encryption key for the disk
questions.why: The identity provider issues a security token that the client presents to apps. Apps trust the token, not the password.

questions.q: Which TWO are pillars of an identity infrastructure?
questions.why: The four pillars are administration, authentication, authorization and auditing.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Authorization happens before authentication.
In a federation, trust between two identity providers is always bidirectional.
Single sign-on lets a user sign in once and access multiple applications.
questions.why: Authentication comes first. Federation trust can be one-way. SSO means one sign-in for many apps.

questions.q: An Azure VM needs to read secrets from Key Vault. You do not want to store or rotate any credentials. What should you use?
questions.why: Managed identities are managed by Azure, so there are no credentials in code or to rotate.

questions.q: A managed identity must be used by five different virtual machines and should exist independently of them. Which type fits?
questions.why: User-assigned identities are standalone and can be shared. System-assigned is tied to exactly one resource.

questions.q: An employee wants to use a personal phone for work email. Which device identity type fits a personal device?
questions.why: Registered is for personally owned (BYOD) devices. Joined and hybrid joined are for organization-owned devices.

questions.q: A company wants on-premises AD users to sign in to Microsoft 365 with the same password, and wants sign-in to keep working if the on-premises servers go down. Which method fits?
questions.why: With password hash sync, authentication happens in the cloud, so it does not depend on on-premises servers. Pass-through and federation both need on-premises components at sign-in.

questions.q: A vendor's staff must access your SharePoint site using their own company accounts. What should you use?
questions.why: B2B collaboration invites external users as guests who sign in with their own identity.

questions.q: Which TWO are workload identities?
questions.why: Workload identities are for software: applications, service principals and managed identities. Guests are human identities.

questions.q: Match each description to the identity type.
rows: An employee's work account
A partner invited as a guest
An app that authenticates to call an API
A company laptop joined to Entra
questions.why: Human identities are workforce or external. Workload identities are for software. Devices have their own identity.

questions.q: A user signs in with a password and a PIN they memorized. Is this multifactor authentication?
opts: Yes, a PIN is something you have
Yes, because two items were entered
No, both are something you know
questions.why: MFA needs factors from different categories. A password and a memorized PIN are both knowledge factors.

questions.q: Which sign-in method is passwordless?
opts: A FIDO2 passkey on a security key
A password plus a voice call
A password plus an SMS code
questions.why: Passkeys (FIDO2), Windows Hello for Business and Microsoft Authenticator phone sign-in remove the password.

questions.q: A small company has no Conditional Access licenses but wants MFA for all users and legacy authentication blocked. What should it turn on?
questions.why: Security defaults give a free baseline: MFA registration for all, MFA for admins, legacy authentication blocked.

questions.q: Help desk calls for forgotten passwords are costing too much. Which feature lets users fix this themselves?
questions.why: SSPR lets users reset or unlock their own accounts after verifying identity.

questions.q: You want to stop users choosing passwords that contain your company name. What should you configure?
questions.why: The custom list holds organization-specific terms. The global list is maintained by Microsoft and cannot be edited.

questions.q: Which TWO are authentication factors that count as something you have?
opts: A registered phone running Microsoft Authenticator
questions.why: A phone or key is something you have. A fingerprint is something you are. A password is something you know.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Windows Hello for Business replaces passwords with a credential tied to the device.
Self-service password reset requires a help desk agent to approve each reset.
The global banned password list is applied automatically to all users.
questions.why: Windows Hello uses a device-bound credential unlocked by PIN or biometrics. SSPR needs no help desk. The global list is automatic.

questions.q: You must require MFA only when users sign in from outside the corporate network. Which feature should you use?
questions.why: Conditional Access applies controls based on signals such as location. Security defaults cannot target conditions.

questions.q: In a Conditional Access policy, what is the user's sign-in location an example of?
questions.why: Signals are the inputs (user, location, device, app, risk). The decision is block or grant. Enforcement applies it.

questions.q: A help desk worker must reset user passwords in Microsoft Entra ID but must not manage Azure virtual machines. Which kind of role should you assign?
opts: An Azure role at subscription scope
questions.why: Entra roles manage directory objects such as users and passwords. Azure roles manage Azure resources.

questions.q: Which role has the broadest permissions across Microsoft Entra ID and should be limited to very few people?
questions.why: Global Administrator can manage everything in Entra ID. Least privilege means few people hold it.

questions.q: Which outcome can a Conditional Access policy NOT produce by itself?
opts: Granting access only from a compliant device
questions.why: Conditional Access blocks or grants access with requirements. It does not delete accounts.

questions.q: Which TWO can be used as signals in a Conditional Access policy?
opts: The size of the user's mailbox
The Azure region of a VM
questions.why: Common signals are user or group, location, device, application and risk.

questions.q: Match each Conditional Access example to its part of the policy.
rows: The user signs in from an unfamiliar country
Grant access, but require MFA
The requirement is applied when the user opens the app
questions.why: Signals are inputs, the decision is block or grant with requirements, and enforcement applies it at access time.

questions.q: Administrators should hold the Global Administrator role only for the hour they need it, after approval. Which feature provides this?
questions.why: PIM gives just-in-time, time-bound, approval-based role activation.

questions.q: Every quarter, group owners must confirm that members still need access, and unconfirmed members should be removed. What should you use?
questions.why: Access reviews recertify access on a schedule and can remove access automatically.

questions.q: A user's credentials are found in a leaked list on the dark web. Which type of risk does Microsoft Entra ID Protection raise?
questions.why: Leaked credentials suggest the identity itself is compromised, which is user risk. Sign-in risk is about a specific sign-in attempt.

questions.q: A sign-in comes from an anonymous IP address in a country the user has never visited. Which risk type is this?
questions.why: Sign-in risk is the probability that a given sign-in was not performed by the identity owner.

questions.q: New project members need a set of groups, an app and a SharePoint site, with access that expires after 90 days. Which feature bundles this?
questions.why: Access packages bundle resources with approval and expiration policies.

questions.q: Which TWO can PIM require before a user activates an eligible role?
questions.why: PIM activation can require MFA, justification and approval, and is time-limited.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Privileged Identity Management provides time-bound access to roles.
Access reviews can only be completed by Global Administrators.
Microsoft Entra ID Protection can feed risk into Conditional Access policies.
questions.why: PIM is just-in-time and time-bound. Reviewers can be owners, managers or the users themselves. Risk is a Conditional Access signal.

questions.q: Admins need to RDP to Azure VMs without giving the VMs public IP addresses. What should you deploy?
questions.why: Bastion provides RDP and SSH through the portal over TLS, so VMs need no public IP.

questions.q: A public website must be protected against SQL injection and cross-site scripting. What should you use?
questions.why: WAF inspects web requests at layer 7 for common exploits. NSGs filter by IP, port and protocol only.

questions.q: You need to allow only port 443 into one subnet and deny everything else. What is the simplest tool?
questions.why: NSGs filter traffic to subnets or network interfaces with allow and deny rules.

questions.q: An application's connection strings are stored in its source code. Where should they be stored instead?
questions.why: Key Vault centrally stores secrets, keys and certificates with controlled, logged access.

questions.q: You need one central, stateful firewall that filters outbound traffic by fully qualified domain name for several virtual networks. What should you use?
questions.why: Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful firewall with application (FQDN) rules, used centrally. NSGs cannot filter by FQDN.

questions.q: Which TWO can be stored in Azure Key Vault?
questions.why: Key Vault stores secrets, keys and certificates.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: A network security group can be associated with a subnet.
Azure Bastion requires each virtual machine to have a public IP address.
Azure DDoS Protection helps keep an application available during a traffic flood.
questions.why: NSGs attach to subnets or NICs. Bastion removes the need for public IPs. DDoS Protection defends availability.

questions.q: Match each need to the Azure service.
rows: Absorb a flood of malicious traffic
Block SQL injection against a web app
Store an API key safely
SSH to a VM with no public IP
questions.why: Each service covers one job: availability under attack, web exploits, secret storage, and secure remote access.

questions.q: Which Defender for Cloud feature gives one number that summarizes your security posture?
questions.why: Secure score is the Defender for Cloud posture measure. Compliance score belongs to Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager.

questions.q: Which standard is applied by default when you enable Defender for Cloud on a subscription?
questions.why: MCSB is the default standard. Others can be added in the regulatory compliance dashboard.

questions.q: You want to find misconfigured resources and get hardening guidance at no extra cost. Which capability provides this?
questions.why: Foundational CSPM is free and provides recommendations and secure score.

questions.q: Management ports on VMs should stay closed and open only when an admin requests access for a short time. Which feature does this?
questions.why: JIT VM access in Defender for Cloud opens ports on request for a limited time.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the Defender plans such as Defender for Servers and Defender for Storage?
opts: Cloud workload protection with threat detection and alerts
questions.why: The Defender plans are the cloud workload protection pillar. They detect threats against specific resource types.

questions.q: Which TWO environments besides Azure can Defender for Cloud protect?
questions.why: Defender for Cloud is multicloud (AWS, GCP) and hybrid. Email and Teams are covered by Defender for Office 365.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: A higher secure score indicates a lower identified risk level.
Security recommendations in Defender for Cloud are generated by assessing resources against security standards.
Foundational CSPM requires a paid Defender plan.
questions.why: Higher score means lower risk. Recommendations come from standards built on Azure Policy. Foundational CSPM is free.

questions.q: Which statement describes a SIEM system?
opts: It collects log data from across the estate, analyzes it and raises alerts and incidents
questions.why: SIEM is security information and event management: collect, correlate, alert.

questions.q: You want Sentinel to automatically disable a user account when a specific incident is created. What should you build?
questions.why: Playbooks are automated response workflows based on Azure Logic Apps.

questions.q: Which Sentinel feature brings in sign-in logs from Microsoft Entra ID?
questions.why: Data connectors ingest data. Analytics rules then detect threats in it.

questions.q: A security analyst wants to search proactively for signs of an attacker before any alert is raised. Which Sentinel capability is this?
questions.why: Hunting is proactive searching with queries. Workbooks visualize, playbooks respond.

questions.q: Which term describes automating the response to security alerts with workflows?
questions.why: SOAR is security orchestration, automation and response.

questions.q: Which TWO describe Microsoft Sentinel?
questions.why: Sentinel is a SIEM and SOAR solution. The CASB is Defender for Cloud Apps.

questions.q: Match each Sentinel feature to what it does.
rows: Data connectors
Analytics rules
Workbooks
Playbooks
questions.why: Connectors collect, analytics detect, workbooks visualize, playbooks respond.

questions.q: Users are receiving phishing emails with malicious links. Which service protects against this?
questions.why: Defender for Office 365 protects email and collaboration from phishing, malicious links and attachments.

questions.q: You want to discover which unsanctioned SaaS apps employees are using (shadow IT). Which service should you use?
questions.why: Defender for Cloud Apps is the CASB that discovers and controls cloud app use. Defender for Cloud protects Azure and multicloud workloads.

questions.q: Which service uses on-premises Active Directory signals to detect lateral movement and compromised identities?
questions.why: Defender for Identity monitors on-premises AD signals. Entra ID Protection detects risk on cloud identities.

questions.q: Which service provides endpoint detection and response (EDR) for laptops and servers?
questions.why: Defender for Endpoint protects devices and includes EDR.

questions.q: Which service continuously finds and prioritizes software weaknesses on devices by risk?
questions.why: Defender Vulnerability Management discovers assets, assesses vulnerabilities and prioritizes by risk.

questions.q: Which TWO are available in the Microsoft Defender portal?
opts: Incidents that combine alerts from several Defender services
questions.why: The Defender portal unifies incidents, alerts and hunting. Labels and retention live in the Microsoft Purview portal.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps is a cloud access security broker.
Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is designed to protect email from phishing.
Microsoft Defender XDR correlates signals across endpoints, identities, email and apps.
questions.why: Cloud Apps is the CASB. Email protection is Defender for Office 365. XDR correlates across domains.

questions.q: Match each Defender service to what it protects.
rows: Defender for Office 365
Defender for Endpoint
Defender for Identity
Defender for Cloud Apps
questions.why: Each Defender XDR service covers one domain, and the portal joins their signals.

questions.q: An auditor asks for Microsoft's SOC 2 audit report for Azure. Where can you download it?
questions.why: The Service Trust Portal publishes independent audit reports and compliance documents.

questions.q: Which Microsoft privacy principle says your email and chat content is not used to target ads?
questions.why: No content-based targeting: personal content is not used for advertising.

questions.q: Which privacy principle is about Microsoft being open about what data it collects and how it is used?
questions.why: Transparency is being open about collection and use. Control is about your choices over the data.

questions.q: On the Service Trust Portal, which feature lets you save documents and get notified when they are updated?
questions.why: My Library pins documents and can notify you of updates.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of Microsoft's six privacy principles?
questions.why: The six are control, transparency, security, strong legal protections, no content-based targeting and benefits to you.

questions.q: Which TWO can you find on the Service Trust Portal?
opts: Penetration test and security assessment reports
Independent audit reports for Microsoft cloud services
questions.why: The portal publishes Microsoft's own compliance evidence. Tenant data lives in your admin portals.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: The Service Trust Portal shows how Microsoft cloud services meet compliance standards.
Under Microsoft's privacy principles, customer content is used to target advertising.
'Control' means customers have tools and choices to manage their own data.
questions.why: The portal provides compliance evidence. Content is never used for ad targeting. Control puts the customer in charge.

questions.q: You must track your organization's progress toward GDPR requirements with recommended actions. Which tool should you use?
questions.why: Compliance Manager has prebuilt assessments for regulations, improvement actions and a compliance score.

questions.q: What does the compliance score measure?
opts: Progress in completing improvement actions that reduce compliance risk
How many resources pass Azure Policy
questions.why: The compliance score reflects completed improvement actions, weighted by risk.

questions.q: In Compliance Manager, a control that Microsoft implements on your behalf is called what?
questions.why: Microsoft-managed controls are Microsoft's responsibility. Your controls are yours. Shared controls are both.

questions.q: Where do you open Compliance Manager?
questions.why: Compliance Manager is a Microsoft Purview solution.

questions.q: Your compliance score is 85%. What does that tell you?
opts: You have completed most recommended improvement actions, but it does not prove legal compliance
You are certified as compliant with all regulations
questions.why: The score measures progress on actions. It is not a certification or a guarantee.

questions.q: Which TWO does Compliance Manager provide?
questions.why: Compliance Manager provides assessments, improvement actions and the compliance score.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Compliance Manager includes templates for regulations and standards.
A high compliance score guarantees that the organization is compliant with a regulation.
Shared controls are implemented by both Microsoft and the customer.
questions.why: Templates create assessments. The score is not a guarantee. Shared controls belong to both.

questions.q: A document must stay encrypted and show a 'Confidential' watermark even after it is emailed outside the company. What should you apply?
questions.why: Sensitivity labels are persistent and can encrypt and mark content. Retention labels control how long content is kept.

questions.q: You need to see that a user copied a labeled file to a USB drive yesterday. Which tool shows this?
questions.why: Activity explorer shows the history of actions on labeled content. Content explorer shows what exists and where.

questions.q: Users must be warned and blocked when they try to email credit card numbers outside the company. What should you configure?
questions.why: DLP detects sensitive information in use and blocks or warns about inappropriate sharing.

questions.q: All email in every mailbox must be kept for seven years and then deleted. What is the simplest configuration?
opts: A retention policy applied to Exchange mailboxes
questions.why: A retention policy applies the same retention settings across a whole location.

questions.q: Which classification method recognizes content such as resumes by learning from example documents?
questions.why: Trainable classifiers use AI trained on examples. Sensitive information types match patterns.

questions.q: Which TWO statements about sensitivity labels are true?
opts: An item can have only one sensitivity label at a time
Labels are removed when a file is emailed
The label stays with the content when it moves
Labels can only be applied by administrators
questions.why: Labels are persistent and one per item. Users apply them, or they are applied automatically.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: A document can have multiple retention labels applied at the same time.
Content explorer shows where sensitive items are located.
DLP policies can show a policy tip to warn users before they share sensitive data.
questions.why: One retention label per item. Content explorer shows location and labels. Policy tips educate users at the moment of sharing.

questions.q: Match each need to the Microsoft Purview capability.
rows: Encrypt and watermark a file
Stop credit card numbers leaving in email
Keep contracts for 10 years
Lock an item so it cannot be deleted
questions.why: Labels protect, DLP prevents leaks, retention governs lifetime, records management locks important items.

questions.q: An employee who has resigned is downloading large numbers of confidential files. Which solution is designed to detect this?
questions.why: Insider Risk Management detects risky activity by insiders such as data theft by departing employees.

questions.q: Legal needs all email and Teams messages about a lawsuit preserved and exported. Which solution should you use?
questions.why: eDiscovery cases let you hold, search and export content as legal evidence.

questions.q: You need to find out which admin changed a mailbox permission last week. Where do you look?
questions.why: The unified audit log records user and admin activities.

questions.q: How long does Audit (Standard) keep audit records by default?
questions.why: Audit (Standard) retains records for 180 days. Longer retention needs Audit (Premium).

questions.q: In eDiscovery, what does placing a hold do?
opts: Encrypts the content with a sensitivity label
Blocks the user from signing in
Preserves content so it cannot be permanently deleted during the case
questions.why: A hold preserves content relevant to a case.

questions.q: Which TWO are Audit (Premium) capabilities?
opts: Retention of audit records for up to 10 years with an add-on
questions.why: Audit (Premium) adds retention policies, longer retention and intelligent insights.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Insider Risk Management pseudonymizes usernames by default.
Audit (Standard) must be manually purchased and turned on before any activity is recorded.
eDiscovery can search content in Exchange mailboxes and Microsoft Teams.
questions.why: Pseudonymization protects privacy. Audit (Standard) is on by default. eDiscovery searches Microsoft 365 locations.

sections.title: Security and compliance concepts
sections.label: High
sections.note: Small domain, but these ideas show up inside questions in every other domain. Two 3D models below.
cold: **Shared responsibility:** you always own **data, devices, accounts and identities**. Microsoft always owns the **physical datacenter, network and hosts**. The middle varies by IaaS, PaaS, SaaS.
**Defense in depth:** seven layers. Physical, identity and access, perimeter, network, compute, application, data.
**CIA triad:** confidentiality, integrity, availability.
**Zero Trust:** verify explicitly, use least privilege access, assume breach. Six pillars: identities, devices, applications, data, infrastructure, networks.
**Encryption:** symmetric = one key, asymmetric = public/private pair. At rest, in transit, in use.
**Hashing:** one-way, fixed length, same input gives same output. Used for passwords, with a salt.
**GRC:** governance (rules), risk management (identify and respond), compliance (follow laws). **Residency** = where data is stored. **Sovereignty** = whose laws apply.
traps: Hashing is not encryption. It cannot be reversed.
'Trust the internal network' is never a Zero Trust answer.
Perimeter (DDoS, edge firewall) vs network (segmentation inside).
hooks: Never trust, always verify.
Know, Have, Are is MFA. Verify, Least, Assume is Zero Trust.

sections.title: Identity concepts
sections.label: Medium
sections.note: Authentication vs authorization is the most common pair on the exam.
obj: Identity as the primary security perimeter
cold: **Identity is the new perimeter** because apps, devices and people are outside the corporate network.
**Four pillars:** administration, authentication, authorization, auditing.
**AuthN** = who are you. **AuthZ** = what may you do.
**Identity provider:** issues security tokens that apps trust. Enables **single sign-on**.
**AD DS** = on-premises directory. **Microsoft Entra ID** = cloud identity provider.
**Federation:** trust between identity providers of different organizations. Not always two-way.
traps: Authentication always comes before authorization.
AD DS is not Entra ID.
hooks: AuthN = who. AuthZ = what.

sections.title: Microsoft Entra ID and identity types
sections.label: High
sections.note: Know each identity type and the three hybrid sign-in methods.
obj: types of identities, including workload identities
cold: **Microsoft Entra ID:** cloud identity and access management. Every Microsoft 365 and Azure tenant has one.
**Identity types:** human (workforce, external), workload (apps, service principals, managed identities), device, and agent identities for AI.
**Managed identity:** Azure manages the credentials. System-assigned = one resource. User-assigned = shared, standalone.
**Devices:** registered (personal), joined (company, cloud), hybrid joined (company, on-premises AD plus Entra).
**External ID B2B:** guests sign in with their own identity.
**Hybrid identity:** Entra Connect Sync or Cloud Sync. Sign-in by password hash sync, pass-through authentication, or federation.
traps: Registered = personal device. Joined = company device.
Password hash sync still works if on-premises is down. Pass-through does not.
Guest users are human identities, not workload identities.
hooks: No secrets in code: managed identity.

sections.title: Authentication in Microsoft Entra ID
sections.label: High
sections.note: MFA factors and passwordless methods are near-certain questions.
cold: **MFA:** two or more of know, have, are.
**Passwordless:** Windows Hello for Business, Microsoft Authenticator, passkeys (FIDO2).
**Security defaults:** free baseline. MFA registration for all, MFA for admins, legacy authentication blocked.
**SSPR:** users reset their own passwords. Fewer help desk calls.
**Password protection:** global banned list (Microsoft, automatic) and custom banned list (your terms). Works for on-premises AD too.
traps: Password plus PIN is not MFA: both are 'know'.
Security questions are for SSPR only, not for sign-in MFA.
A Windows Hello PIN never leaves the device.
hooks: Know, Have, Are.
sections.modTitle: Describe the authentication capabilities of Microsoft Entra ID

sections.title: Access management in Microsoft Entra
sections.label: High
sections.note: Conditional Access: signal, decision, enforcement.
obj: Microsoft Entra roles and role-based access control (RBAC)
cold: **Conditional Access:** if-then policies. **Signals** in (user, location, device, app, risk), **decision** (block or grant with requirements), **enforcement**.
**Entra roles** manage Entra resources (users, groups, apps). **Azure roles** manage Azure resources (VMs, storage).
**Built-in** roles are ready-made. **Custom** roles need a premium license.
**Least privilege:** the smallest role that does the job.
**Global Secure Access:** Entra Internet Access and Entra Private Access (Security Service Edge).
traps: Global Administrator is an Entra role. Owner is an Azure role.
Security defaults and Conditional Access are not used together.
hooks: Conditional Access = if this, then that.
sections.modTitle: Describe access management capabilities of Microsoft Entra

sections.title: Identity protection and governance
sections.label: High
sections.note: Four tools that get mixed up: ID Governance, access reviews, PIM, ID Protection.
cold: **ID Governance:** right people, right access, right resources, right time. Entitlement management uses **access packages**.
**Access reviews:** regularly confirm who still needs access. Remove what is not confirmed.
**PIM:** just-in-time, time-bound, approval-based activation of privileged roles.
**ID Protection:** detects **user risk** (identity compromised) and **sign-in risk** (this sign-in is suspicious). Remediates with risk-based Conditional Access.
traps: Leaked credentials = user risk. Anonymous IP or atypical travel = sign-in risk.
PIM activates roles. Access reviews recertify them.
hooks: PIM = admin only when needed.
sections.modTitle: Describe the identity protection and governance capabilities of Microsoft Entra

sections.title: Core infrastructure security in Azure
sections.label: High
sections.note: Overlaps with AZ-900 Domain 2. Know which service does which job.
obj: network segmentation with Azure virtual networks
cold: **DDoS Protection:** keeps apps available during traffic floods. Network Protection (per VNet) or IP Protection (per public IP).
**Azure Firewall:** managed, stateful, central firewall. Filters by IP, port and FQDN.
**WAF:** protects web apps from SQL injection and cross-site scripting. On Application Gateway or Front Door.
**VNets** isolate. **Subnets** segment inside a VNet.
**NSG:** allow and deny rules by priority on a subnet or network interface.
**Bastion:** RDP and SSH from the portal over TLS. No public IP on the VM.
**Key Vault:** secrets, keys, certificates.
traps: NSG cannot filter by domain name. Azure Firewall can.
WAF is for web apps (layer 7). Azure Firewall is for network traffic.
Just-in-time VM access is Defender for Cloud, not Bastion.
hooks: Bastion = the safe gate to your VMs.
sections.modTitle: Describe core infrastructure security services in Azure

sections.title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud
sections.label: High
sections.note: Posture (CSPM) vs protection (workload plans).
obj: enhanced security features provided by cloud workload protection
cold: **Defender for Cloud:** CNAPP covering Azure, AWS, GCP and on-premises.
**CSPM:** finds misconfigurations, gives recommendations. **Foundational CSPM is free.** Defender CSPM is paid.
**Secure score:** higher is better.
**Microsoft cloud security benchmark** is the default standard. Standards are built on Azure Policy.
**Workload protection:** paid Defender plans (Servers, Storage, Containers, Databases and more) that raise security alerts.
**JIT VM access:** opens management ports only on request, for a limited time.
traps: Secure score is Defender. Compliance score is Purview.
Defender for Cloud is not Defender for Cloud Apps.
hooks: Posture = how well set up. Protection = catching attacks.
sections.modTitle: Describe the security management capabilities in Azure

sections.title: Microsoft Sentinel
sections.label: Medium
sections.note: Know SIEM vs SOAR and which Sentinel feature does what.
obj: security information and event management (SIEM) and security orchestration automated response (SOAR)
threat detection and mitigation capabilities in Microsoft Sentinel
cold: **SIEM** collects and correlates. **SOAR** automates response. **Sentinel is both**, cloud-native.
**Collect** (data connectors), **Detect** (analytics rules), **Investigate** (incidents, hunting), **Respond** (playbooks).
**Playbooks** are built on Azure Logic Apps.
**Workbooks** are dashboards.
Sentinel now lives in the **Microsoft Defender portal**.
traps: Workbook shows. Playbook acts.
Sentinel is not a CASB and not an endpoint tool.
hooks: Collect, Detect, Investigate, Respond.
sections.modTitle: Describe security capabilities of Microsoft Sentinel

sections.title: Threat protection with Microsoft Defender XDR
sections.label: High
sections.note: The largest group in the largest domain. One job per Defender service.
cold: **Defender XDR:** joins signals across endpoints, identities, email and apps into one incident.
**Defender for Office 365:** email and collaboration. Phishing, Safe Links, Safe Attachments.
**Defender for Endpoint:** devices. EDR.
**Defender for Cloud Apps:** CASB. Shadow IT and SaaS control.
**Defender for Identity:** on-premises Active Directory signals.
**Defender Vulnerability Management:** find and prioritize weaknesses.
**Defender Threat Intelligence:** who the attackers are and how they work.
**Defender portal:** security.microsoft.com.
traps: Defender for Identity = on-premises AD. Entra ID Protection = cloud identities.
Defender for Cloud Apps (SaaS) is not Defender for Cloud (Azure workloads).
hooks: Office = email. Endpoint = device. Identity = AD. Cloud Apps = SaaS.
sections.modTitle: Describe threat protection with Microsoft Defender XDR

sections.title: Service Trust Portal and privacy principles
sections.label: Medium
sections.note: Short stop. Memorize the six principles.
cold: **Service Trust Portal:** Microsoft's audit reports, certifications and compliance guides. My Library saves documents.
**Six privacy principles:** control, transparency, security, strong legal protections, no content-based targeting, benefits to you.
traps: The Service Trust Portal shows Microsoft's compliance, not yours.
Transparency = Microsoft tells you. Control = you decide.
hooks: Microsoft runs on trust.
sections.modTitle: Describe Microsoft's Service Trust portal and privacy principles

sections.title: Compliance management in Microsoft Purview
sections.label: Medium
sections.note: Compliance Manager and its score.
obj: uses and benefits of compliance score
cold: **Purview portal:** purview.microsoft.com.
**Compliance Manager:** assessments from regulation templates, improvement actions, compliance score.
**Controls:** Microsoft-managed, your controls, shared.
**Compliance score:** risk-based progress on improvement actions. Not a guarantee of compliance.
traps: Compliance score is not secure score.
A high score is not a certificate.
hooks: Compliance Manager = your to-do list for regulations.
sections.modTitle: Describe the data compliance solutions of Microsoft Purview

sections.title: Information protection and data lifecycle
sections.label: High
sections.note: Sensitivity labels, DLP and retention are asked from many angles.
obj: sensitivity labels and sensitivity label policies
retention policies, retention labels, and retention label policies
cold: **Classification:** sensitive information types (patterns) and trainable classifiers (learned from examples).
**Content explorer** = what exists and where. **Activity explorer** = what was done to it.
**Sensitivity labels:** persistent, can encrypt and mark content. One per item. Published with label policies.
**DLP:** stops sensitive data leaving through email, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive and devices.
**Retention policy** = whole location. **Retention label** = one item. One retention label per item.
**Records management:** lock important items and review before disposal.
traps: Sensitivity label protects. Retention label keeps or deletes.
Content explorer vs Activity explorer.
hooks: Know, Protect, Prevent, Govern.
sections.modTitle: Describe the data security solutions of Microsoft Purview

sections.title: Insider risk, eDiscovery and audit
sections.label: Medium
sections.note: Three tools for investigations.
cold: **Insider Risk Management:** risky activity by insiders. Usernames pseudonymized by default.
**eDiscovery:** find, hold and export content as legal evidence.
**Audit (Standard):** on by default, 180 days.
**Audit (Premium):** one year by default for core services, up to 10 years with an add-on, retention policies.
traps: eDiscovery hold is for a legal case. Retention policy is general.
Audit answers 'who did what, when'.
hooks: Insider = people. eDiscovery = evidence. Audit = activity.

duels.clue: One-way. Cannot be reversed to get the original.
duels.why: Hashing is one-way and fixed-length. Encryption can be reversed with the right key.

duels.clue: Uses a public and private key pair.
duels.why: Asymmetric uses a key pair. Symmetric uses one shared key.

duels.clue: Data falls under the laws of the country where it is held.
duels.why: Sovereignty is about which laws apply. Residency is about where data may physically be stored.

duels.clue: Segment access and monitor so an intruder cannot spread.
duels.why: Assume breach minimizes blast radius. Verify explicitly checks every request on all available signals.

duels.clue: Decides what you are allowed to do.
duels.why: Authorization grants access levels. Authentication proves identity.

duels.clue: Cloud identity provider built for modern authentication.
duels.why: Entra ID is cloud-based. AD DS is the on-premises directory.

duels.clue: A trust between identity providers of different organizations.
duels.why: Federation is the trust. SSO is the one-sign-in experience it can enable.

duels.clue: Deleted automatically when its one resource is deleted.
duels.why: System-assigned shares the lifecycle of one resource. User-assigned is standalone.

duels.clue: Organization-owned device signed in with a work account.
duels.why: Joined is for organization-owned devices. Registered is for personal devices.

duels.clue: Password is validated by an on-premises agent. Nothing stored in the cloud.
duels.why: Pass-through validates on-premises. Password hash sync stores a hash of the hash in Entra.

duels.clue: You add your own company and product names.
duels.why: Custom holds your terms. Global is maintained by Microsoft.

duels.clue: Free baseline that turns on MFA for everyone with no policy design.
duels.why: Security defaults are preset and free. Conditional Access gives granular if-then policies and needs a premium license.

duels.clue: A fingerprint or face scan.
duels.why: Biometrics are something you are. Phones and keys are something you have.

duels.clue: Owner, Contributor and Reader on a resource group.
duels.why: Those are Azure RBAC roles for Azure resources. Entra roles manage directory objects.

duels.clue: Block access, or grant access with MFA.
duels.why: Block and grant are decisions. Signals are the inputs such as user, location and risk.

duels.clue: Reach internal company apps without a traditional VPN.
duels.why: Private Access is for private apps. Internet Access secures internet and SaaS traffic.

duels.clue: Activate an admin role for two hours with approval.
duels.why: PIM handles just-in-time activation. Access reviews recertify existing access.

duels.clue: Atypical travel detected on one sign-in.
duels.why: Atypical travel relates to a specific sign-in. User risk is about the identity being compromised.

duels.clue: Detects leaked credentials and risky sign-ins.
duels.why: ID Protection detects and remediates risk. ID Governance manages who has access and for how long.

duels.clue: Managed stateful firewall, central, can filter by FQDN.
duels.why: Azure Firewall is the central, fully featured firewall. NSGs are basic allow and deny rules on subnets or NICs.

duels.clue: Stops SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
duels.why: WAF protects web apps at layer 7. Azure Firewall filters network traffic generally.

duels.clue: Secure RDP and SSH from the portal.
duels.why: Bastion is remote access. Key Vault stores secrets, keys and certificates.

duels.clue: Billed per protected public IP address.
duels.why: IP Protection is per public IP. Network Protection covers a virtual network.

duels.clue: Finds misconfigurations and gives hardening recommendations.
duels.why: CSPM is posture. Workload protection detects active threats on specific workloads.

duels.clue: Shown in Microsoft Defender for Cloud.
duels.why: Secure score is Defender for Cloud. Compliance score is Purview Compliance Manager.

duels.clue: Paid. Adds attack path analysis.
duels.why: Defender CSPM is the paid plan with attack paths and agentless scanning.

duels.clue: Automates response workflows.
duels.why: SOAR automates the response. SIEM collects and correlates logs.

duels.clue: Runs an automated response built on Logic Apps.
duels.why: Playbooks act. Workbooks display data.

duels.clue: Cloud-native SIEM and SOAR.
duels.why: Sentinel is the SIEM/SOAR. Defender for Cloud is posture management and workload protection.

duels.clue: Cloud access security broker for SaaS apps.
duels.why: Cloud Apps is the CASB. Defender for Cloud is CSPM and workload protection for Azure, AWS and GCP.

duels.clue: Monitors on-premises Active Directory signals.
duels.why: Defender for Identity watches on-premises AD. ID Protection covers Entra cloud identities.

duels.clue: Safe Links and Safe Attachments.
duels.why: Those are Defender for Office 365 features for email and collaboration.

duels.clue: Threat actor profiles and indicators of compromise.
duels.why: Threat Intelligence describes attackers. Vulnerability Management finds weaknesses in your own assets.

duels.clue: Download Microsoft's ISO and SOC audit reports.
duels.why: The Service Trust Portal holds Microsoft's audit reports. The Purview portal is where you manage your own compliance.

duels.clue: Microsoft is open about what it collects and why.
duels.why: Transparency is openness. Control is your ability to manage the data.

duels.clue: Your files and email are not used for ads.
duels.why: That is no content-based targeting. Security is protecting data with strong safeguards and encryption.

duels.clue: Progress toward meeting regulations such as GDPR.
duels.why: Compliance score is about regulations. Secure score is about security posture.

duels.clue: You implement it yourself.
duels.why: Your controls are customer-managed. Microsoft-managed are done by Microsoft.

duels.clue: Tracks your own improvement actions.
duels.why: Compliance Manager manages your compliance. The Service Trust Portal shows Microsoft's evidence.

duels.clue: Controls how long content is kept before deletion.
duels.why: Retention labels govern lifetime. Sensitivity labels classify and protect.

duels.clue: History of what users did with labeled files.
duels.why: Activity explorer is the history. Content explorer is the current inventory.

duels.clue: Applies at item level, such as one document.
duels.why: Labels are per item. Policies cover a whole location.

duels.clue: Pattern matching, such as a credit card number format.
duels.why: Sensitive information types use patterns. Trainable classifiers learn from examples.

duels.clue: Keeps records up to 10 years with an add-on license.
duels.why: Premium extends retention. Standard is 180 days.

duels.clue: Find and export evidence for a legal case.
duels.why: eDiscovery is for legal evidence. Insider Risk Management detects risky user activity.

duels.clue: Preserves content tied to a specific legal case.
duels.why: Holds are case-based. Retention policies apply broadly for compliance.
